title: SFI26 update: Window 1 now closed

content.content: Window 1 of the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26)  has now closed. Thank you to everyone who took the time to submit an application.
As planned, this application window remained open for 2 months before closing. The remaining Window 1 budget will be made available through Window 2.

We have seen strong interest in the scheme and are grateful to all those who chose to apply in this window. We will now continue to process the applications received, and eligible applicants will be offered agreements in due course.
If you receive an agreement offer, please make sure you accept it within 30 calendar days, or the offer will be withdrawn.
If you were eligible to apply but did not submit an application during Window 1, there will be another opportunity when Window 2 opens, which is expected to open on 22 September.
Started but not submitted applications
Some eligible farmers started an application but did not submit it before Window 1 closed.

We recognise that farmers have many demands on their time, so most of these Window 1 "started but not submitted" (SNS) applications will remain on the system. This means applicants will be able to complete and submit them when Window 2 opens.
The Rural Payments Agency (RPA) will contact these applicants shortly to explain the next steps.
However, some farmers with a Window 1 SNS application will need to start a new application when Window 2 opens. This applies where RPA has had to withdraw the original application because:
RPA's communication to affected farmers will explain what they need to do and why a new application is required.

The approach of retaining most Window 1 SNS applications on the system so applicants can complete and submit them when Window 2 opens, applies only to Window 1 of SFI26. It does not set a precedent for how SNS applications will be handled in Window 2 of SFI26 or in future SFI application rounds. We will confirm the approach for Window 2 in due course.
Window 1 figures at a glance
In this post, I'd like to share some headline figures from Window 1.
To remind you, Window 1 was designed to prioritise smaller farm businesses and those without an existing ELM revenue agreement.

We did this to ensure that farms with fewer opportunities to access support were among the first to benefit from the offer. We saw strong interest from the types of businesses that Window 1 was designed to support.

These figures are based on the applications we received, and the information provided by applicants at the point of application. They do not reflect final agreement figures, as applications are still being processed.
Numbers have been rounded to help illustrate the overall picture and should be treated as indicative rather than exact.
Application profiles
Approximately 6,500 applications were submitted during Window 1.

The average annual agreement value in Window 1 was just under £10,000. This indicates that funding is being successfully distributed across a larger number of farmers, rather than concentrated among a smaller number of high-value recipients.
Top 5 actions
Applicants selected actions across all 14 SFI26 action groups, reflecting the flexibility of the scheme and the diversity of farming businesses taking part.
The most popular actions were:
CLIG3: Manage grassland with very low nutrient inputs

The benefits of this action extend beyond biodiversity. When established alongside cropped land, species-rich grasslands can support the natural processes that underpin resilient food production. Flower-rich habitats provide resources for pollinators and other beneficial insects, while diverse vegetation offers shelter for species that contribute to natural pest regulation. These areas can also slow surface water movement, reducing soil and nutrient losses and helping to retain valuable resources within the farmed landscape.
CHRW2: Manage hedgerows

Well-managed hedgerows can support the natural processes that contribute to resilient food production. Flowering hedgerows provide resources for pollinating insects, while their shelter and habitat benefits encourage populations of beneficial invertebrates that can contribute to natural pest regulation and integrated pest management. Hedgerows can also help reduce wind erosion, slow surface water movement and improve the retention of soil and nutrients within the farmed landscape.
GRH7: Haymaking supplement

This action aims to produce a crop of field-dried hay that is grown and harvested in a way that allows wildflowers and grasses to flower and set seed naturally. This traditional management approach helps to conserve the diverse plant communities found in hay meadows, while also providing valuable sources of pollen and nectar for bees and other pollinating insects. In addition, it contributes to improved water quality and supports the maintenance of traditional landscape character, helping to preserve the environmental and cultural value of grassland habitats.
CSAM3: Herbal leys
This action aims to maintain an established herbal ley containing a diverse mixture of grasses, legumes, herbs and wildflowers that provide varied root structures throughout the soil profile.

The ley should include areas of flowering plants from late spring through the summer months, supporting biodiversity and providing valuable resources for pollinators and other wildlife. The purpose of this mixture is to produce a high volume of forage while minimising the need for inorganic fertilisers, improving resilience to drought, and helping to enhance and maintain the soil’s structure, carbon content, biological activity and overall fertility.
WBD1: Manage ponds

The purpose of this action is to increase biodiversity, improve water quality and provide valuable habitat for native aquatic species. Healthy ponds can also contribute to sustainable farming by helping to retain and filter water within the landscape, reducing soil and nutrient loss from surrounding land, supporting pollinators and natural pest predators, and improving the overall environmental resilience of the farm.
Processing times
The RPA continues to process applications as quickly and efficiently as possible.
While some applications require additional checks and can therefore take longer to assess, applications are progressing well overall.
On average, applicants are currently receiving an agreement offer within 24 days of submitting their application.
Of the approximately 6,500 applications, the RPA has issued around 3,615 agreement offers so far, helping farmers move forward with their activities sooner.
Looking ahead to Window 2
We expect Window 2 to open from 22 September for all eligible farmers and land managers.
Before you start an SFI26 application for Window 2, read the ‘Get ready to apply’ guidance in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance.
It explains the steps you need to take before you start your application, so the process is as straightforward as possible.
This includes making sure that the land parcels you want to include in your application are shown correctly on your digital maps in advance.
If these land details are not correct, it may prevent you from applying for SFI26. Please be aware that mapping updates may impact any existing ELM revenue agreements you already have.
Video support
The RPA made a step-by-step video that guides you through the application process, so you know exactly what to expect.
Please check that your digital maps show the correct details for any land parcels you want to include in your SFI26 application.
You should also make sure your land use information is up to date, as this is managed by you through the Rural Payments service. Any updates must be completed before you submit your application.
The RPA also created a series of how-to videos to help you update your digital maps.
The RPA has been gathering feedback from Window 1 applicants about their experience, and will make improvements for Window 2, wherever possible.

In addition, a range of measures to support farmers through current drought conditions was recently announced. This includes an additional £50 million for Window 2 of SFI26, bringing the total scheme budget to £290 million for this financial year.
By enabling more farmers to take up SFI actions, we can help businesses improve their resilience to future droughts while delivering benefits for food production and the environment.
Beyond SFI26

Looking beyond SFI26, ministers have committed publicly to stabilising the main design of SFI for the duration of this Parliament so that farmers and land managers know what to expect in the years ahead.
In keeping with the commitments made in the Farming Roadmap 2050, we plan to offer an SFI27 scheme in 2027.
Following Window 2 of SFI26, we will consider whether any refinements are needed for SFI27 and will share information on these as early as possible.
Subscribe to the Farming Blog
We'll continue to share updates on the Sustainable Farming Incentive as they are available.
Subscribe to the Farming Blog and you'll receive a notification whenever we publish a new post.

description: Window 1 of the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) has now closed. We expect Window 2 to open from 22 September. This post provides an overview of figures and insights from Window 1.

title: OTSI Blog post – Annual Review 2025-2026

content.content: The Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) has published its Annual Review for 2025-26. OTSI was launched in October 2024 as part of wider efforts to enhance the effectiveness of UK sanctions in supporting domestic and global security.

This Annual Review reflects on the breadth of OTSI’s activities over the 2025-26 financial year in supporting compliance through our extensive engagement, guidance and outreach programme as well as licensing, and in tackling non-compliance by assessing breach reports received, taking forward enforcement action and further developing intelligence-led casework.

As our figures show, implementing and enforcing the Russia sanctions regime has been a key focus for OTSI in 2025-26. We continue to see Russia going to ever greater lengths to try to obtain the goods and services necessary to fuel its illegal war in Ukraine. OTSI, as the UK’s dedicated, expert trade sanctions implementation body, is committed to taking the actions necessary to disrupt malign activity and to promote the importance of compliance and due diligence.

We continue to build on the foundations we set in 2025-26. The implementation of new Sanctions End-Use Controls in May this year marks an important expansion of OTSI’s powers to tackle circumvention. This comes alongside the expansion of OTSI’s licensing remit in April to include exports of sanctioned goods and ancillary services.

As ever, OTSI welcomes our stakeholders’ feedback and engagement; we continue to strive to ensure that businesses receive a high-quality and efficient service. Upcoming sanctions workshops across the UK will offer businesses, in particular small and medium-sized businesses which may be less confident in navigating trade sanctions, opportunities to learn more about sanctions compliance and get practical support. In addition, we always welcome queries or comments via our webpage.

title: A day in the life of a Fisheries Enforcement Officer

content.content: For most anglers, a Fisheries Enforcement Officer is the person who checks their fishing licence. But for the Environment Agency, the work of our enforcement officers helps protect fisheries, wildlife and the future of angling.
From routine patrols and licence checks to investigations and protecting vulnerable fish species, Fisheries Enforcement Officer Richard takes us behind the scenes of a day in his life.
Planning the patrol
Patrols often begin long before we reach the water.
We are guided by intelligence, local knowledge and valuable reports from anglers, members of the public and partner organisations.

Before we head out on our patrol, we check our intelligence system to see if there's any relevant information for that area including previous offending, hotspot locations, recorded incidents and information from other enforcement partners like the police. We then tailor our patrols to that intelligence.
We're out every day on some sort of water, no matter the weather.
Licence checks on the bank
When we get to any location, whether it be a river or a lake, we have to record the time we arrive in our pocket notebook; it's a legal document and can be used in court to provide evidence.
As we carry out rod licence checks, we show our authorisation as we go. Hopefully they'll all be happy and enjoying themselves and catching fish legally!

The rod licence money that anglers pay goes back into fishing in a number of different ways. For example, fishery owners can have Environment Agency specialists out to assist and advise them on potential issues before they become bigger issues, we also invest a lot of that income back into fishing and angling through schemes like the Fisheries Improvement Programme, which supports environmental and habitat improvements as well as making fisheries more accessible and safer and helping to bring new anglers into the sport – especially youngsters.
Following up reports
Licence checks are just one way fisheries enforcement officers help protect fisheries and tackle illegal fishing.
Illegal fishing can come in many forms. Reports from members of the public help us investigate incidents, build intelligence and respond to threats to fisheries and wildlife.

One issue is traps and other illegal instruments. We've seen all kinds over the years, from children's fishing nets all the way up to seine nets, cast nets and gill nets, the latter of which tangle fish up so they cannot get out of them.

While we are out, we keep an eye out for set lines. These are lines attached to the bank and a stake with bait on a hook. These can be set quite sneakily to avoid us finding them. Plastic bottles and tin cans are often used to identify where traps have been laid.

These lines are then left for a few hours before someone comes back to them. They can catch any fish species and wildlife other than fish and are particularly damaging to the environment and other kinds of wildlife.

We remove these illegal traps and once retrieved, equipment may be recorded, photographed and retained as evidence to help officers investigate incidents and take action where offences have occurred. We can also stake-out locations known to be hotspots, with the aim of catching offenders red handed.
Protecting fisheries and wildlife
This is only one side of fisheries enforcement. No two days are ever quite the same, and across England our officers are tackling very different challenges.

From routine patrols to specialist operations, the work may look different, but the aim is the same. We gather intelligence and monitor activity across our waters - teams may also use specialist equipment, including drones and night-time surveillance tools, to gather evidence and support investigations.

Some specialist operations focus on protecting migratory fish such as Atlantic salmon and sea trout - our officers cover every watercourse and even up to 6 nautical miles out into the sea to carry out vessel checks for migratory fish species. When fish populations are already under pressure, tackling illegal fishing can help protect some of our most vulnerable fish species.
Find out more

Most people will only ever see a small part of fisheries enforcement. Behind every patrol are intelligence-led operations, incident responses and specialist work helping to protect fisheries, wildlife and angling for future generations.

If you see illegal fishing activities on any inland water report in England, contact the Environment Agency’s Incident Hotline immediately on 0800 80 70 60 (available 24/7) or use the official online Report an Environmental Problem tool.
Watch our day in the life of a Fisheries Enforcement Officer video and find out how to buy a fishing licence.

title: A guide to keeping kids healthy this school year for parents and carers

content.content: As children head back to school and we move closer to winter, now is a good time to familiarise ourselves with some of the common illnesses that can cause disruption to children’s time in school during the colder months.

This blog post covers some of the seasonal illnesses that tend to rise during autumn and winter, as well as steps you can take now and throughout the coming term to help protect your family, including from cold weather. We’ll explore available vaccinations, how to recognise symptoms of common illnesses, and how to make informed decisions on whether a sick student is well enough to attend school or college.
Teach good hygiene habits
Good hygiene stops infections from spreading, which means less disrupted learning time.

Teach your child to wash their hands thoroughly with soap and warm water, use tissues for coughs and sneezes, and stay away from others when sick. Letting in fresh air can also reduce the spread of airborne viruses. Our e-bug resources for all ages can help you to explain and discuss hygiene habits – and why they are important – to your child or teenager.
Know when to keep your child at home
The start of a new term is a good time to familiarise yourself with the symptoms of common illnesses:
The NHS has a useful guide to help parents decide whether a child is well enough to go to school, based on their symptoms.
Know how to spot the signs

There are other types of illnesses to watch out for at this time of year, including bacterial infections such as scarlet fever. Although we see cases throughout the year, they usually peak in the late winter and early spring.

The most common symptoms of scarlet fever include sore throat, fever, swollen neck glands, a bumpy rash on the chest and tummy with a sandpaper-like feel, flushed cheeks and ‘strawberry tongue’. If you suspect your child has scarlet fever, contact your local GP. Stay away from nursery or school for 24 hours after the first dose of antibiotics.

Since autumn 2023 there have been a number of major measles outbreaks in the West Midlands, North West and London, with sporadic cases across the country – in 2024, England saw the highest number of measles cases  since 2012. Outbreaks have continued in 2025 and 2026. Measles can be a very serious disease for some children and tragically it can even cause fatalities. The initial symptoms of measles are similar to those for a cold (runny nose; a cough; sneezing; a high temperature; and red, sore, watery eyes) this is followed by white spots in the mouth a few days later, and by a rash on the face and body a few days after that. It's very unlikely to be measles if your child has had both doses of the MMR/MMRV vaccine or they’ve had measles before. Viral infections such as chickenpox can also spread in schools at any time of year and are highly contagious. An itchy, spotty rash is the main symptom of chickenpox. It can be anywhere on the body.
Ensure your child is up to date with vaccinations

Vaccines provide the best protection against many common but potentially serious illnesses. Over the past decade, fewer children are getting routine vaccines, putting them at risk of serious disease. This leaves schools vulnerable to outbreaks and increases pressure on the NHS.

If your child is up to date with their NHS vaccination schedule, they will already be protected against diseases like whooping cough, measles, mumps and rubella throughout their time at school, as most provide lifelong immunity.

Unvaccinated children are at higher risk of contracting these illnesses and having more severe symptoms than vaccinated classmates. They can also spread diseases to others. Check your child’s red book or contact your GP practice to ensure they are up to date on all vaccines.
School-age children and young people are offered the following vaccinations:
Protect your child from the cold

Low indoor temperatures can have a serious impact on children’s health. Children under the age of 5 are particularly vulnerable. However, the effects of cold, especially in combination with other environmental conditions including damp, can affect children of all ages and particularly those with underlying medical conditions.
UKHSA guidance gives advice on a range of actions you can take to protect your child from cold weather, including:
Financial support is also available to help manage the costs of heating your home, especially for those on low incomes. The government has published energy saving tips to help save money on bills.
Through these preventative measures, and by recognising illnesses promptly, you can help your child stay healthy and keep school absences to a minimum this term.

title: Listening, learning, changing: my first update to driving instructors

content.content: This is my first direct message to you since becoming DVSA Chief Executive and I wanted to take this opportunity to focus on a few issues I know matter greatly to many of you as driving instructors.
This blog post is also a longer read than what we’d normally publish, but please, stick with it, because I think it has some really important information for you.
Getting out and about and listening

Since I started at DVSA, I've spoken directly with driving instructors, learner drivers, examiners and other DVSA colleagues about how life-changing the driving test is. I've also read through what you told us in last year's ADI survey, including the harder messages.

Many of you told us that DVSA asks for feedback and then does not show what changes as a result. Many of you commented on DVSA's management and policy, saying we have not done enough to address the backlog. And fewer than 4 in 10 of you feel you get the chance to contribute your views before decisions are made that affect you. I take that seriously and I think it has, at times, been a fair criticism. I'll come back to what we're doing about it.

What has struck me most in my visits is the professionalism and commitment shown by instructors across Great Britain. I've met instructors managing their own waiting lists, having the difficult conversation of telling a pupil they are not ready and seeing their professional advice undermined by others telling them to “give it a go”.
I know this has not just been a professional frustration. It has hit your ability to plan, disrupted your diaries and added challenges to a job you find meaningful.

Your survey responses were clear on this: pupils putting lessons on hold for months, the stop-start cycle of filling gaps with new pupils only for former pupils to return at short notice and the near-impossible task of managing demand you cannot control. I do not underestimate the impact that this has had on you.
Long driving test waiting times are not simply an inconvenience for learners either. For some, they delay the next step in their education or career. They can affect:

Behind every driving test is someone trying to take the next step in their life and behind every instructor is a small business trying to plan around a system that has, for too long, made planning very hard.
That is why reducing waiting times remains my top priority.

I'm not going to pretend this can be fixed overnight. Waiting times remain too long in many parts of Great Britain. But DVSA is working hard to improve the situation as quickly as possible and I want to be open about the progress we're making, the challenges that remain and the changes we're introducing as a direct result of what we've heard from you.
Focus on ADI qualification tests and standard

I've also heard clearly from the industry and people who want to become an instructor, or are already registered, that the long waiting times for a part 2 or 3 test or a standards check are unacceptable. This is having a negative impact on the driver training industry, those working to join it and the trainers or organisations sponsoring them.

While the focus of this blog post is around what we’re doing to tackle waiting times for learners, I want to reassure you that we are also looking at ways to improve our ADI services. Our Director of Enforcement, Marian Kitson, will provide an update soon on what we’re doing in this space.
Progress is being made, but this is not fixed
There are signs that the situation is beginning to improve and I want to show you the evidence rather than just assert it.
On 30 March 2026, 182 driving test centres were showing 24 weeks' wait in the booking service. By 27 July 2026, that had reduced to 143.

The measure we use for weeks until at least 10% of weekly appointments are available improved from 22.1 weeks at the end of March to 20.7 weeks at the end of July. However, the national median waiting time between booking and taking the test increased from 9.0 weeks to 11.1 weeks. This increase was expected as the unofficial ways of finding earlier tests were closed down.
The percentage of appointments still available to book has increased from 7.7% to 11.8% over the same period.
And the latest published data shows that in July 2026, DVSA completed 197,295 driving tests, the highest monthly total we have ever recorded. That was:

These figures show movement in the right direction. But waiting times are still not good enough and I recognise that. Progress is not being felt evenly everywhere: some test centres and regions are seeing far less improvement than others. Many instructors and learners are still living with the impact of long waits every day and I will not pretend otherwise.
What's changed since March, and why
Since March, we've introduced a range of changes designed to make the booking service fairer and easier to manage.

We introduced these measures because too many learners were losing out to people misusing the booking service. Tests were being held, swapped, sold or resold in a way that made it harder for genuine learners to get an appointment. That was not fair to learners. It was not fair to you, supporting them. And it was not right for a public service to allow it to continue.
Here is what we've done:

These changes are starting to contribute to the improvements in availability I've described, but they are not the only cause. They sit alongside a wider package of work on examiner recruitment and overtime.

It will be 3 months since we brought the changes in in September. Our lead for driving test waiting times Christian Oreschnick will write a blog post giving you a more detailed look at what the data is telling us and plans to move examiners into areas where waiting times are highest.
I do need to be clear about one thing: these reforms are not going to be undone. They were introduced to increase fairness and stop exploitation and that principle stands.

But introducing changes at pace means listening, learning and improving as we go. Some things have worked well. Some things need improving. We will not shy away from telling you that as the evidence comes in.
Recruiting more examiners
Alongside the booking reforms, we've continued to recruit driving examiners and make use of overtime to increase testing capacity.

As of July 2026, we had 157 more full-time equivalent driving examiners in post than a year earlier, an increase of 10.9%. As a direct result, we have conducted over 120,000 more driving tests in the first 4 months of this financial year than over the same period last year.
I know that many of you have told us, repeatedly, that recruiting and retaining examiners should be DVSA's central focus.
I’m changing 3 things because of what you have told us

One of the clearest messages I have heard from you is that DVSA asks for feedback but does not always show clearly what changes as a result. I recognise that this has happened. I want to change it, starting with these 3 things.
1. Better guidance to help learners find a test

Today we are publishing new guidance to help you and your pupils better understand how driving test availability actually works. We've heard from many people who believe all appointments are released at 6am on Monday mornings. This leads to large queues to get into the service.

In reality, appointments become available at different times and for different reasons throughout the week. This guidance will not solve waiting times, but it should reduce confusion and help to get the Monday morning queue working more efficiently.
2. A way for learners who need additional support to appoint someone to deal with DVSA on their behalf
We've heard concerns from the industry about learners who need additional support and may struggle to manage a booking themselves.

We plan to work with The Association of Disability Driving Instructors, NASP, charities and learners who need additional support to build and test a new way for eligible learners to formally appoint someone to speak to DVSA on their behalf regarding their driving test booking.
We’ll update you further on the details on this work in future.
3. Letting you see Ready to Pass? emails sent to your pupils
Another thing many of you have told us is that it can be difficult to reinforce messages when you cannot see exactly what DVSA is sending to your pupils.

As driving instructors, you are the professionals who work with learners week in, week out. You understand their strengths, weaknesses and readiness better than anyone else. So it's important that you can see the information and advice we are providing alongside your lessons.

That's why today we've published copies of every Ready to Pass? campaign email in the driving instructor toolkit. These are refreshed versions and we will start to send them from 1 September 2026. You can now see what learners receive, when they receive it and how the messages align with different stages of the learning journey.

You will see that the emails consistently encourage learners to trust their instructor's judgement, develop all of the skills needed for safe driving and think carefully about whether they are genuinely ready before taking a test. They reinforce the message that passing the test is not the goal in itself; becoming a safe driver for life is.
Unfortunately, we cannot copy instructors into emails when they are sent, as they contain personal data.

However, where we can be more transparent, we should be. Publishing these emails means you can see exactly how we're supporting the conversations you're already having with your pupils, and how we're encouraging learners to value your professional expertise.

This builds on the wider changes we've recently made to the Ready to Pass? campaign, including the focus on the 27 driving skills and helping learners think about readiness in terms of safe, independent driving rather than simply passing a test.
Being more transparent

I believe we should be open about our performance, whether the news is good or bad. That's why we've started publishing more detailed information about driving test waiting times and availability, including data at individual test centre level.
You can see where progress is being made, where challenges remain and whether the actions we're taking are leading to results.
Greater transparency means greater accountability, and that is good for DVSA, instructors and learners alike.
What happens next

We will continue to recruit and train more driving examiners, make use of overtime, publish more detailed performance data, prevent misuse of the booking service and improve the service where evidence shows changes are needed.
Thank you for the important role you play in helping people become safe and competent drivers and for your patience while we work to make this system work better for you.

title: Lightweight architecture for learning at pace
authors: Pete Hallett, Head of Technology, CustomerFirst

content.content: Why architecture became about people, not technology
When we started building the technology and architecture practice for CustomerFirst, we thought we had a reasonable idea of the role architecture would play.
Like many teams, we expected to spend our time understanding technology estates, mapping systems, identifying technical risks and leading organisations towards making good technology decisions.

What we did not expect was that the most valuable architectural conversations would have very little to do with technology at all. Instead, we've found ourselves talking about organisations, relationships and trust. We've spent time understanding how decisions are really made, where operational boundaries exist, and how information moves between teams. We’ve also explored why seemingly simple changes can become surprisingly difficult.

As we've worked with different organisations, we've realised these themes aren't unique to one partner. They've appeared repeatedly across services and departments, changing the way we're thinking about architecture.

Before committing to significant investment or large-scale transformation, we work with organisations to understand whether a different approach is actually viable. We test ideas, gather evidence and learn quickly before deciding what should happen next; we’ve previously written about our approach to exploration sprints. We're also learning what it takes for multidisciplinary teams to succeed in the NewCo model, and architecture needs to fit that environment.
As we've written before, NewCo is about creating bounded space for small, multidisciplinary teams to look at a service differently.

Many architectural approaches were developed for delivery programmes that already knew where they were heading. We're often working with organisations that are still defining the problem, or where the problem itself has evolved. They're exploring options rather than implementing predetermined answers, which has prompted us to rethink architecture's role in delivery.

If understanding the landscape takes months, teams lose the ability to learn quickly. If decisions have to pass through layers of governance, momentum fades and support for change becomes harder to build.
None of this invalidates traditional approaches to enterprise architecture. It simply reflects the context it was designed for. We're finding ourselves applying architecture differently.
What we mean by lightweight architecture

We've started referring to this as lightweight architecture. This is not because it reduces the rigour required to meet core principles of scalability, secure by design, interoperability or maintainability. It’s because it applies just enough architectural thinking to help teams make the next good decision. Rather than answering every question up front, it helps teams move forward with confidence while leaving room for new evidence to influence future decisions.
What we learned from two recent engagements
During a recent six-week discovery, we worked across an extremely fragmented and complex federated landscape.
At the outset we expected much of the work to be on technology and integration, to understand the systems, the dependencies and how everything connected.

We quickly discovered that understanding the technology was only one part of the challenge. The more important learning was understanding the landscape around it: who owned what, where decisions were made, how change happened and what would need to be true for services to evolve safely.
Users in this context do not experience those organisational boundaries; they experience a moment as part of their wider journey across that complex system.

That observation changed the conversations we were having. We spent less time discussing integration patterns and more time building a shared understanding of the problem, identifying operational dependencies and exploring how information could be shared responsibly. These conversations were every bit as architectural as discussing platforms or APIs.
One of the most valuable architectural decisions we made on another engagement was not deciding what to build. It was deciding not to build at all.

Instead of investing immediately in technology, we created a small experiment that generated evidence within days. The experiment was simple to implement, however went through a fast-tracked but fully signed-off governance process to get the experiment safely in front of users.

We worked with the Data Protection Officer as part of the delivery loop rather than as an approval gate. By giving them early access to the architectural decisions they were quickly able to assess risk and resolve privacy concerns that needed assurance before launch and within the scope of the experiment.

We used existing products that have been built and exist in the GDS products suite. We obtained approval to divert a small segment of user data that flowed into the service for a particular cohort of users. We used technical expertise from the partner organisation to route the cohort to the new service and worked with content designers so the new service could be found by that group during the experiment.

That evidence is now shaping future decisions in a way that simply would not have happened had we started with a detailed solution and spent weeks or even months working through governance processes designed for larger-scale change. We know governance systems exist to reduce risk in delivery. We are testing the application of appropriate governance at varying stages of our work, which is important, especially as we move towards higher fidelity, where more governance and assessment will always be necessary.
Reducing the cost of discovering the future

Experiencing high governance environments has reinforced something we'd started to suspect across several explorations: perhaps one of the most valuable things architecture can do is not describe the future but reduce the cost to the taxpayer of discovering the future. That idea continues to shape our thinking.

We're not presenting lightweight architecture as a finished methodology or a replacement for established architectural practices. But the faster organisations need to learn, the more architecture itself needs to become adaptive.

For us, that means architecture becoming another enabling function within the CustomerFirst model. It helps teams understand before they invest, helps partners work before they integrate, and helps organisations make confident decisions while uncertainty still exists.

description: CustomerFirst shares what two years of architecture practice has taught them about people, trust and lightweight governance, and why less can be more.

title: Sign up for seminar exploring the future of cervical screening in the era of HPV vaccination

content.content: The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) is pleased to invite stakeholders to the latest in its series of online seminars aimed at increasing public awareness of the complexities and nuances of screening.
From vaccination to elimination: HPV and the future of cervical screening will take place on Wednesday 30 September 2026 from 3.30pm to 5.00pm.
Registration will close at 12pm on Wednesday 30 September 2026 (BST).
Further details, including joining instructions, will be sent out to registered attendees nearer the event.
From vaccination to elimination: what the evidence tells us

A recently published study led by Professor Peter Sasieni has examined cervical cancer mortality trends in England following the introduction of HPV vaccination. The findings add to a growing body of evidence on the impact of HPV vaccination programmes and what they could mean for efforts to eliminate cervical cancer in England and beyond.

As HPV-vaccinated cohorts move through the NHS Cervical Screening Programme, important questions are emerging about the future of screening. How is cervical cancer risk changing? What role will innovations such as HPV self-sampling play? How might cervical screening evolve in a vaccinated population while continuing to protect those most at risk?

This seminar will explore the findings of Prof Sasieni’s research alongside wider developments in cervical screening, vaccination and cancer prevention. Speakers will discuss the current cervical screening programme, delivery of HPV vaccination, emerging evidence on cervical cancer risk, and what the future may hold for cervical screening policy and practice.
The seminar will be hosted by Professor Anne Mackie and will feature presentations from:
Attendees will also have the opportunity to take part in a question-and-answer session with the speakers.

The seminar is likely to be of particular interest to screening professionals and programme leads, public health specialists, clinicians and healthcare practitioners, researchers and academics, patient and public representatives, charities and voluntary organisations.
About our seminars

The UK NSC regularly hosts seminars to encourage discussion of important developments in screening policy and practice. These events are designed to support learning, share emerging evidence and encourage engagement with stakeholders from across the screening community.

title: Dragons' Den IP Blog - Series 23 Episode 9

content.content: A seedy snack range and a water-saving device – two pitches that caught my attention as guest Gary Neville took his seat beside seasoned Dragons, Touker Suleyman, Deborah Meaden, Steven Bartlett and Peter Jones.
Sowing the seeds of a growing business
Did you know, more than 90% of people in the UK don’t eat enough fibre?

Chester Robinson, founder of Raise Snacks, wants to help by ‘elevating’ peoples’ snacking experience by (in Chester’s words) “celebrating nuts and seeds”. He explained how he enhances these functional foods, which are full of protein, fibre and anti-oxidants, with the addition of ingredients such as chocolate, raspberry and caramel which result in tasty and original Raise Snacks ‘clusters’.

Asked if the snacks were truly healthy, Chester explained how he was “trying to meet that sweet spot between taste and health” for modern day snackers. I can relate to that, thinking back to the times I’ve needed a health bar boost  on a walk or bike ride, but have closed my eyes to the sugar content.
When it comes to the crunch…

An attractive proposition (stocked by Sainsburys and Leon, about to launch in Ocado, the recipient of a £95k grant from entering a competition with Sainsburys), Chester received offers from all the Dragons. He had a difficult  decision to make.

Ultimately, Chester shook hands with the two Dragons he had hoped for, for  a share each of  10% for £50k. Gary Neville (“you’re driven, smart, likeable, authentic”) and  Steven Bartlett (“I come to the Den looking to meet people like you”) looked excited at the prospect of helping Chester seize opportunities in what  Steven described as an emerging fibre story.
Raise the brand
Chester has registered three trade marks: Raise Snacks, RAISE and BARK.

A trade mark will allow  you to use your brand name, logo, or other distinctive  elements without the risk of  imitation by competitors.  Find out more about what you can trade mark here: Register a trade mark : What you can register as a trade mark - GOV.UK
Water way to prevent waste!
After a summer that has seen the whole of Wales and a large percentage of England officially in drought, news of Jason and Belle Robinson’s water-saving device was timely.

The enthusiasm bubbling from Belle made for a compelling pitch. She  described how much time she was wasting, standing beside buckets and troughs on their farm, waiting for them to be filled with water for their horses.  The alternative? She could head off to do something else in the 25 minutes it takes to fill the trough but runs the risk of it overflowing – not just a waste of water but a mucky mess in the yard.

All that thinking time waiting for the fill has obviously paid off, as the couple have come up with Sealstop – a portable, fully automated, easy to use  product that will stop the flow of water from a hose once the container is full. So simple but so effective.

Belle and Jason were asking for 50k in return for 7% equity. To date they have sold more than 1,200 units with a turnover of £45k and a net profit of minus £7,500k. Jason is still working long hours as a farrier and assembling the  Sealstop device at home, while Belle admitted to only paying herself enough to cover her National Insurance.
“Jason keeps us afloat!” she quipped.

Belle stands her ground  The Dragons clearly warmed to the lively and likeable pair, but all thought the £39.99 retail price was high. Like a horse refusing a hurdle, Belle stood her ground at suggestions they could have had the device made cheaper  elsewhere, extolling the quality of the injection-moulded product which is  manufactured local to their Yorkshire home. “It has to last”, she said, adding that it was priced in line with other quality hose accessories on the market.
Horse-owner Deborah could relate to the problem, agreeing that with 4 horses herself, taking 3.5 minutes to fill each bucket meant a lot of time wasted. But at that price…?
The dry facts

Belle was ready for the challenge, telling how water authorities want to drop  the average daily consumption from 144 litres per person to 110:“A bath is 80 litres of water. People are going to have to think about water saving”.

When we’re being told we can make a difference just turning the tap off to  clean our teeth, Belle has a point. The pair received plenty of compliments  but one by one, the Dragons turned down the opportunity to invest, citing  too narrow a market and too high a price point.

A potential oasis in a desert of declines, Deborah asked if the couple would consider licensing Sealstop. They were unsure, as they were concerned about the loss of control over the device into which they had poured heart and soul. One last drop of advice was available, however - Deborah said if they were ever considering it, to talk to her about it.
How would licensing work?

With a bit of research, I could see that the Robinsons not only have a  registered Sealstop trade mark (trade mark UK00003874218) but they also have a registered design (Design 6137959 Liquid flow control device) both of which would help if the couple decide on licensing:

A trade mark gives you the exclusive right to use your brand in the area in which you register it, preventing others from using anything similar in that field.  As well as IP protection, it can enhance the visibility of a brand which can attract potential investors or licensees, which can assist with scaling up.
A registered design can give the owner an enforceable right to using the design. This can help prevent competitors from unauthorised use of the design, unless under licence.
Find out more about licensing your IP here: Licensing intellectual property - GOV.UK.

title: Your guide to who’s eligible for the autumn 2026 flu vaccine

content.content: Flu season is approaching, and some people can already book their free NHS flu vaccine. Here's everything you need to know about who can get vaccinated this year and what's changed since last autumn.
What's new for autumn 2026?

There are 2 notable changes this year. First, some community pharmacies will be able to offer flu vaccinations to more children. Last year, some community pharmacies offered flu vaccines to 2- and 3- year olds for the first time. From 1 October 2026, some pharmacies can also vaccinate children aged 2 years to less than 18 years who are in clinical risk groups. This runs alongside the existing offer given in schools and GP practices, which starts from 1 September 2026. From 1 December 2026, some pharmacies will also help catch up any school-aged children who missed their vaccination via the schools teams. These changes are designed to help make it easier for families to access the vaccine at a time and place that suits them.

Second, rough sleepers and those using homeless hostels or night-shelters, aged 16 years and over, are now included in the national flu programme for the first time, from 1 October 2026. This follows advice from the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI).
Who is eligible for the flu vaccine this year?
From 1 September 2026, the following groups are eligible. Where ‘clinical risk groups’ are mentioned, these are defined in the Green Book, Influenza Chapter:
From 1 October 2026, the following groups become eligible:
Why does flu matter?

Flu is far more than a bad cold. It can lead to serious complications such as bronchitis and pneumonia, worsen existing health conditions, and in severe cases lead to hospitalisation or death. Because the flu virus changes each year, the vaccine is updated annually, so it's important to get vaccinated even if you had the vaccine last year.
How is the vaccine given?
Adults are usually offered the vaccine as an injection. Most children are offered a nasal spray instead.
Can the vaccine give you flu?

Most children receive a nasal spray vaccine rather than an injection. It's offered to children because it works well, has an excellent safety record, and is quick and painless. The spray contains a live attenuated (weakened) influenza virus that helps protect against flu. Parents sometimes worry this 'live' vaccine might cause flu in their child. The weakened virus does not cause flu in children who receive it. Only children who are severely immunosuppressed (such as those who have just had a bone marrow transplant) may be advised by a doctor to avoid live vaccines. Millions of doses have been given in the UK and across the world.

Unvaccinated contacts are not at risk from being near a recently vaccinated child, whether in the same room during vaccination or afterwards. There's no need for any child or staff member to be excluded from school during vaccination sessions or in the following weeks. The tiny number of children who live with very immunosuppressed people, may be offered an alternative injected flu vaccine.
When and how can I get vaccinated?

If you're eligible, the NHS will usually contact you to tell you when you can book. For parents of most school-aged children this will be via their school. If you think you're eligible but don’t hear anything, speak to your GP practice, pharmacist, or, if you're pregnant, your midwife.

The best time to get vaccinated is in autumn or early winter, before flu starts spreading widely. If you miss this window, it's still worth getting vaccinated later, as flu activity can continue throughout winter.

title: Adopting a user-centred design approach to our internal content landscape

content.content: Content is one of the most important assets in an organisation. It shapes decisions, supports services and helps colleagues get things done. That’s why we’ve established the Content Improvement team, a digital function focused on making sure our internal content, tools and platforms are accessible and user-friendly, and meet the needs of all our colleagues.

By taking a user-centred design (UCD) approach to our internal content landscape and treating content as critical infrastructure, rather than just a communications tool, we’re supporting our digital strategy objective to enhance operational excellence and drive organisational efficiency, helping our department deliver better outcomes.
In this blog post I share what we are doing and why we are doing it.
Internal content as critical infrastructure

Earlier this year, after the redesign of our department intranet, I partnered with a user researcher colleague on a discovery to better understand our department’s wider internal content landscape. This included content held across internal platforms such as SharePoint, ServiceNow, Teams and Confluence.

I expected to uncover duplication, outdated pages and opportunities for improvement, but it quickly became clear that this wasn’t the main problem. This was simply the visible symptoms of a deeper, common challenge across many large organisations: a fragmented ecosystem of platforms, ownership and lack of consistent central governance and culture surrounding content.

We often think of content as something that sits on a website, but in reality, it underpins how people make decisions, complete tasks and deliver services. If content is essential to how an organisation functions, then it is not just a communications asset. It is part of our internal infrastructure, and organisations should treat it that way.
What we discovered about our content landscape
The discovery phase helped to better understand the challenges facing our internal content landscape.

We examined our existing content ecosystem in depth, speaking to content owners and platform users, gathering feedback through surveys, and mapping user journeys across key internal platforms. This helped us to identify pain points and uncover recurring themes.

These challenges spread across multiple internal platforms, where content may be duplicated and not always clearly owned or maintained. Teams were publishing content without shared standards, governance or specialist support, making it harder to create a coherent, consistent and accessible content landscape. This increased the risk of outdated information, inconsistent user experiences and accessibility barriers for colleagues trying to find and use the information they needed.

Furthermore, as artificial intelligence (AI) tools become a bigger part of everyday work, well-structured, accessible and standardised content is essential. High-quality content not only improves the user experience for colleagues but also enables AI tools to surface, interpret and reuse information more accurately and effectively.
The role of the Content Improvement team

Internal content might not attract the same attention as external services, but it has a direct impact on how effectively we work. An outdated page, duplicated process or unclear instruction creates friction for colleagues. Over time, that friction becomes wasted effort and unnecessary demand on support teams.

For years, organisations have invested heavily in creating content. Far fewer have invested in managing it. That’s why governance matters. Good governance isn’t about bureaucracy. It’s about making sure content remains accurate, owned, findable and useful long after it’s published.

Our team exists to improve the quality, consistency and sustainability of our internal content estate. We work alongside and support existing teams with content best practice, good governance and accessibility. Our job is to fix systemic issues, not through tactical tidying, but through a strategic, department‑wide approach.

We sometimes joke that we’re part content designer, part detective and part content police. We spend our time tracing ownership, uncovering duplicate information and investigating why colleagues can’t easily find what they need. Ultimately though, our mission is simple:
Our 3-phase model
The following 3 phases provide an overview of our approach:
Phase 1: Set the standards
In phase 1, we want to create a clear, unified approach to provide a single source of truth that the whole department can adopt.
Before fixing anything, we need to define what “good” looks like.
What we’re doing
Good practice scales thanks to shared rules. Phase 1 builds the foundations for everything that follows.
Phase 2: Fix the past
The largest phase is about cleaning up legacy content. Phase 2 is not a one‑and‑done exercise. It’s a systematic transition to a sustainable, well‑governed ecosystem.
What we’re doing
Phase 3: Futureproofing (ongoing)

When the estate is clean and effectively governed, we shift into long‑term sustainability. This phase is focused on raising the standards of internal content – it's not a short-term fix, but a strategic investment in content built to last.
What we’re doing
What this means for colleagues
The impact of our work will be felt across teams through:
The Content Improvement team wasn’t created to fix individual pages. It was created to embed the foundations of good content at scale.

As the project progresses, we will aim to share what we learn and the impact of our work. If you work on similar challenges across government and are interested in learning more about our work, get in touch.
Join our team!

description: The Content Improvement team in MHCLG focuses on making sure internal content across our platforms is accessible and user-friendly, and meets the needs of all colleagues. By treating content as critical infrastructure rather than just a communications tool, we’re helping our colleagues, and the AI tools they use, work more efficiently.

title: Explore More for Less: Affordable South East Nature Days Out

content.content: This summer, if you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the South East!

Whether you're after a gentle walk or a long trek, wonderful wildlife or ancient history, the South East has it all. It's tough to narrow it down, but here are some of our favourite days out for you to enjoy!
The King Charles III England Coast Path at Chichester Harbour
Enjoy a stretch of the King Charles III England Coast Path around Thorney Island, taking in stunning views of Chichester Harbour – all within reach of Chichester and Portsmouth.

This 8-mile route begins in the picturesque village of Emsworth and ends at Southbourne, though can be completed in either direction, and passes by special saltmarshes, mudflats and dune habitats. The fully waymarked coast path offers the chance to spot seals, coastal wildflowers and birds including terns, redshanks, curlews and ospreys. Remember, if seal or birdwatching at the coast make sure to keep your distance and not cause any disturbance!

From Emsworth you can join the coast path at Queen Street, on the eastern side of the island you can join at Prinsted Lane in Prinsted. If you fancy an even bigger challenge this stretch forms part of over 200 miles of coast path that is now open across Hampshire & Sussex!

Please be aware that Thorney Island is an active army base. There are two security gates on either side of the island where you will be required to use an intercom system to gain onward access. Always check the National Trails website in advance of your walk to check for any temporary MOD closure notices.
Getting there: You can catch the train from Chichester or Portsmouth to Emsworth. If you're doing the full 8-mile stretch, catch the train home from Southbourne.
Hindhead Commons, part of the Wealden Heaths National Nature Reserve (National Trust)
Across Surrey, Hampshire & West Sussex is a 2,440 hectare patchwork of some of England's most important ancient heathlands - the Wealden Heaths National Nature Reserve.

Hindhead Commons & the Devil's Punch Bowl, one of twenty sites across Wealden Heaths, is the perfect spot to enjoy what the NNR has to offer. Devil's Punch Bowl offers spectacular views of the colourful heath landscape. Named for the local legend of the Devil scooping and throwing dirt at Thor, the Punch Bowl has an onsite cafe with toilet facilities and is a short step-free walk from a car park and bus stop.

Hindhead Commons is home to a well waymarked walking routes from which you may see sunbathing reptiles, including sand lizards and adders, blooming heather plants, and if you're lucky, and visit near dusk, the rare nightjar bird.
With the ongoing hot and dry weather, please remember to act responsibly while in natural spaces. This NNR's heathland is especially vulnerable to wildfires, so please do not light fires or BBQs.
Getting there: Take the number 19 bus from Haslemere Railway Station. Haslemere is a short train journey from both Godalming and Guildford.
Mount Caburn National Nature Reserve near Lewes
Take in spectacular views of the South Downs from Mount Caburn National Nature Reserve - a  short trip from Brighton.

Used since the Iron Age as a base for fortifications, the south facing chalk hill and valley of Mount Caburn's chalk grassland, a globally rare habitat, is home to wildflowers and diverse range of butterflies and moths. Its wildlife includes burnt-tip, common and pyramidal orchids as well as Adonis blue butterflies, silver-spotted skippers and scarce forester moths.

The flora and fauna of Mount Caburn have flourished due to traditional grazing practices used for thousands of years across the South Downs. These management methods are still used to maintain the grassland today. The conditions required to create this habitat mean wildlife is particularly susceptible to human disturbance, so please remember to take litter home with you and to leave no trace of your visit.
Getting there: Catch the Brighton to Eastbourne/Hastings train and get off at Glynde. Alternatively, for a longer walk, start at Lewes and head eastwards up Chapel Hill onto the South Downs.
Thames Path National Trail
Spanning 185 miles, the Thames Path National Trail passes through historic towns and cities, peaceful water meadows, bustling riverside communities and our capital.

Starting at the source of the Thames, to the west of Cirencester, the full 185-mile route crosses 8 counties and takes you all the way to Woolwich in East London. If you don't fancy the full challenge, there are plenty of great short routes along the way.

Enjoy a 9-mile stretch from Oxford to Abingdon: beginning at Folly Bridge, the route takes you past Christ Church Meadow and onwards past Iffley Lock and into the Oxfordshire countryside where the river passes meadows and farmland. Keep an eye out for waterbirds, such as kingfishers, and dragonflies including the Southern Hawker.

Another great spot to join the Thames Path is Henley-on-Thames. This beautiful Georgian town is a relaxed spot to enjoy riverside pubs and a laidback stroll along the river. Henley is also home to an interactive mural celebrating 30 years of the Thames Path which you can find at Mill Meadows Pavillion.

London has many starting points to offer, from leafy riverside nature of Richmond, the hustle & bustle and iconic views of the City, to the maritime history of Greenwich. Through London the path, mostly, covers both banks of the Thames so there are ample opportunities for creating your own circular route.
Plan your own trip, and find information on any diversions, by visiting nationaltrail.co.uk
Getting there: For the Oxford to Abingdon route, catch the train to Oxford. To return to Oxford take the bus from Abingdon.
For Henley catch the train from Twyford which is reachable direct from London Paddington and Reading.
If walking the full route from west to east catch the train to Kemble and then the 882 bus to Smerrill Quarry,  a 30 minute walk from the start of the route. Return from Woolwich station.

If you are visiting the coast, rivers or other open water, check local conditions, weather and tide times, follow safety signs and choose a lifeguarded beach where possible. Consult with  Tide Times to help plan your visit, and read up on water safety advice before you set out.

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999.
Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature!

title: Biodiversity Net Gain for major infrastructure projects – new guidance

content.content: From 2 November 2026, Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) will become mandatory for new nationally significant infrastructure project (NSIP) applications in England.
Bringing BNG into the NSIP system is an important next step for nature. It will ensure that much needed major infrastructure is delivered while also protecting and restoring nature at scale.

To help developers prepare, we have today published guidance setting out how BNG should be considered throughout the design and consenting process. The guidance builds on the final biodiversity gain statements and initial guidance published earlier this year, details of which were set out in our June blog.

Covering all NSIP sectors, the guidance explains how BNG requirements can be met, encouraging developers to consider BNG from the earliest stages of project design and engage with relevant stakeholders to inform their proposals.
The guidance also delivers on the recommendations of the Nuclear Regulatory Taskforce Review to introduce a streamlined BNG framework for NSIPs, which means:
The guidance can be viewed here:  Biodiversity net gain: nationally significant infrastructure projects - GOV.UK
We encourage NSIP developers to familiarise themselves with the guidance, feedback on it, and use it to support the preparation of their applications ahead of 2 November 2026.
Further guidance changes for BNG
We have also updated two existing BNG guidance pages to improve their useability and clarify how they apply to NSIPs as well as planning applications:
What’s next for BNG?
As set out in our July blog, the first phase of BNG reforms for smaller sites, including the 0.2 hectare exemption, came into force on 6 August 2026.
Work is underway on the second phase of reforms which include:

We will also make some changes to the statutory biodiversity metric. These include measures to address some of the specific challenges that BNG can pose for brownfield developments with open mosaic habitat, and changes to the way spatial risk is assessed for area habitats by using Local Nature Recovery Strategy areas only.
These changes will require the statutory metric act paper to be amended and laid before Parliament, and we will confirm timings and further details in due course.
We will provide transitional arrangements and guidance for projects using the current statutory biodiversity metric when the updated metric is introduced.
Brownfield consultation
The consultation on a potential additional targeted exemption for certain residential brownfield development closed on 10 June 2026.
All responses and evidence submissions are being analysed and the Government will respond to the consultation in due course.

title: Explore More for Less: Affordable Southwest Nature Days Out

content.content: If you’re looking for fun and accessible days out that are low-cost, then we have you covered. Not only is spending time in nature great for your wellbeing, it can also be great for your bank balance. Here are our suggestions for our favourite affordable days out in the Southwest!

The Southwest is packed with incredible places to explore, many of them completely free. Whether you're looking for riverside strolls, family-friendly wildlife watching, rockpool adventures, rocky scrambles or spectacular wildflower meadows, there's plenty to discover.
For wildlife, history and hands-on exploration: The Avalon Marshes Centre and Somerset Wetlands National Nature Reserve

The Avalon Marshes Centre is the perfect hub for a family day out. Enjoy a picnic near the wildlife pond and make use of the amenities – including a visitor information point, café and accessible toilets – as well as visiting the on-site museum and craft gallery. Throughout the summer, they host family friendly events that connect people with the wildlife and history of the site. From there, it’s a short walk to Shapwick Heath National Nature Reserve, a gateway to the Somerset Wetlands here you can follow pushchair-friendly paths or ancient tracks. Lucky visitors might catch a glimpse of the resident beavers or sparkling kingfishers and dragonflies.

Getting there: The 668 weekday bus service connects the Avalon Marshes Centre with nearby towns and villages. It is also linked to Glastonbury, Street and Wedmore by quiet lanes and cycle paths. The centre is around 10 minutes by car from Glastonbury and has free parking on site with donations encouraged.
For a classic day out by the sea: Weymouth Beach, Dorset

For a proper day at the seaside, this award-winning stretch of golden sand is perfect for building sandcastles and paddling in the gentle waves. A stroll along the sweeping seafront connects you to the King Charles III England Coast Path where adventurous visitors can extend their day with a walk. Head east from Weymouth for a challenging cliff-top climb and panoramic sea views, or head west for an easier walk towards the unique landscape of Chesil Beach and Fleet Lagoon, a rare habitat and the largest saltwater lagoon in the UK.
Getting there: Weymouth station is just a short hop from the beach. Weymouth is also well connected to nearby towns by bus and there are plenty of car parks, including a park and ride service.
For accessible trails across diverse wildlife habitats: Goss and Tregoss Moors, part of the Mid Cornwall Moors NNR

Goss Moor features heathland, wetlands, pools and scrub habitats. A largely level seven-mile multi-use trail provides easy access for walkers, cyclists and families, with Tramper, equestrian, and cycle accessible gates.

Home to some of the country’s rarest species such as lesser butterfly orchid, yellow centaury, marsh clubmoss and Cornish moneywort. The 29 species of butterfly and 18 species of dragonfly and damselfly include the nationally scarce small red damselfly. Dormice reside in grassy open areas and the reserve is a stronghold for Britain’s fastest declining resident bird, the willow tit. The moor is surrounded by medieval farms and the characteristic remains of tin-streaming and gravel extraction.

Getting there: The nearest train stations to Goss Moor are in St Columb Road and Roche. Bus services run close to the reserve from St Austell to Newquay and from St Columb Major to Bodmin. See the Tradeline SW website for details.
For coastal adventures: Wembury and the King Charles III England Coast Path, Devon

Few places combine coastal scenery and wildlife quite as well as Wembury. Managed by the National Trust and part of a voluntary Marine Conservation Area, Wembury Beach is widely regarded as one of the best places in the UK for rockpooling.

At low tide, families can discover an extraordinary variety of marine life, including sea anemones, crabs, starfish and small fish hidden among the rocks. The Devon Wildlife Trust’s Wembury Marine Centre helps visitors learn more about the area's rich marine environment through displays, events and guided rockpool safaris (free or for a small charge).

Beyond the beach, the South West Coast path, which has been improved and is now part of the King Charles III England Coast Path. Here you will find spectacular walks, such as the popular ⁠Wembury to Heybrook Bay Walk with views across Plymouth Sound and out to the iconic Great Mewstone island.

Getting there: The No.48 bus runs from Plymouth city centre. The Yealm ferry (for foot passengers and bikes) runs between Noss Mayo, Newton Ferrers and Wembury between 1st April and 30th Sept. By car follow the A379 through Elburton, then signs to Wembury Beach. The car park can fill quickly so arriving early is recommended.
For wildflowers and butterflies: Pewsey Downs National Nature Reserve, Wiltshire

The steep sunny slopes of Pewsey Downs are the perfect place to spot butterflies dancing among colourful wildflowers this summer. Keep your eyes peeled for the electric Adonis Blue fluttering past and keen noses might catch the rich scent of wild thyme and marjoram drifting on the breeze. With spectacular views stretching across to Salisbury Plain, you can also get up close to the Alton Barnes White Horse, one of the eight famous white horses still visible in Wiltshire today. These hills are not for the faint-hearted, however, so a visit here may suit families with older children more than little ones in buggies.
Getting there:  Pewsey Downs has a free car park near Alton Barnes village (Postcode SN8 4LU) and buses from Pewsey train station run to Alton Barnes, about one mile south of the reserve.
For rocky scrambles and epic views: Ebbor Gorge, Mendip Hills

Not far from its famous cousin, Cheddar Gorge, is the lesser known but equally impressive Ebbor Gorge. Paths wind their way through the dramatic limestone cliffs while small streams and rocky climbs make for exciting scrambling. Make it to the top and you will be rewarded with stunning views across the landscape. See if you can spot the willow bear sculpture lurking in the woods, representing the beasts that once roamed these lands, and the many fossils that have been found in the local caves.
Getting there: There is a free car park at the gorge, which is locked at dusk (Postcode BA5 1AY).
For an oasis in the city: Urban nature walks in Truro, Cornwall

For walks close to the city centre, Daubuz Moor offers riverside meadows, wetlands, wildflowers and woodland along the River Allen ideal for pushchairs, wheelchairs and short family walks. Coosebean Woodland has riverside paths, woodland trails and open green spaces. Visit Truro also has suggestions for stunning coast and countryside walks within 10 miles of Truro.

Getting there: Daubuz Moor is a 5-10 min walk north from Truro Cathedral to the gate on Moresk Road. For Coosebean Woodland follow the riverside path upstream from near Victoria Gardens or cross the footbridge from Truro railway station. Gate at the end of St George’s Road. Or use Coosebean Lane for a pram- or wheelchair-friendly path.
A few more favourites
We can’t mention everything so here are a few more of our favourite low cost, accessible places to visit in the South West this summer.

If you are visiting the coast, rivers or other open water, check local conditions, weather and tide times, follow safety signs and choose a lifeguarded beach where possible. Consult with  Tide Times to help plan your visit, and read up on water safety advice before you set out.

With the recent dry, hot weather, wildfire risk is high across the countryside. Please pack a picnic instead of a barbecue, take your rubbish home with you, and if you spot an unattended fire, get to a safe place and call 999.
Remember to always follow the Countryside Code when you’re out and about in nature!
