title: How science is helping us respond to the Tyne nurdle pollution incident

content.content: By Dr Rob Bradburne, Environment Agency Chief Scientist
When incidents happen, good decisions depend on good science.

That is certainly true of the ongoing recovery along North East England's coast, where a maritime collision released small pellets of plastic, known as nurdles, and other debris into the Tyne estuary and along surrounding beaches. The spill has taken a significant toll on local communities, with residents facing the distress of seeing treasured beaches polluted and spending many hours helping to protect and clean up their coastline.

Our operational teams and partners are working to assess and manage pollution on the ground. Building on the excellent early advice provided in the immediate aftermath, a committee of scientists from across and beyond the Defra group, called the Scientific and Technical Advice Committee, is providing evidence that underpins every aspect of the ongoing recovery operation.

As chair of the committee, I’ve seen just how important scientific collaboration is during uncertain and rapidly developing situations. From modelling the movement and risks of nurdles to advising which clean-up approaches could be most effective, the team draws on a wide range of expertise. Together we’re considering the best available science, advising those managing the recovery so that they can make choices to protect nature, wildlife and coastal communities.

Nurdles are small pellets of plastic used as the raw material for manufacturing plastic products. Following a maritime incident, nurdles and associated debris entered the estuary and marine environment and began washing up along the coastline.
While the pellets may appear small and relatively harmless, they could present significant environmental harm if they remain in the environment in large quantities.

One of the committee’s biggest challenges is understanding where the nurdles have gone and where they may move next. We’re bringing together modelling, monitoring and expert judgement to build the clearest possible picture. Already, scientists spotted where nurdles travelled upstream, prompting industry funding to explore the estuary’s dynamics in greater detail.
This evidence helps responders consider where nurdles may be present in the environment and which habitats or locations may need closer attention as the incident develops.

One of the most important roles of science during an incident is identifying where risks are greatest. While evidence on the environmental impacts of nurdles is still developing, the committee is working at pace to point out potential risks as the situation unfolds.

Scientists are highlighting the potential vulnerability of protected coastal habitats including saltmarsh, mudflats, seagrass and vegetated shingle. These habitats support internationally important wildlife and can be particularly difficult to clean once plastic material becomes embedded within them. We’re also considering the implications for seabirds, marine mammals, fisheries and other coastal species.

Beyond the immediate impacts of pollution, the committee is advising on when to end the clean-up effort. Digging up large areas of beach could damage the habitats that we’re trying to protect. Our advice helps responders balance the benefits of recovery against the risk of further environmental harm.

During the ongoing recovery, the scientific committee is providing evidence-based recommendations on issues such as monitoring the material in the marine environment, protecting particularly sensitive habitats and prioritising clean-up efforts. This includes advising the Recovery Coordination Group on how to define the limits of the recovery process so they can move confidently into planning the next phase of recovery.

I’ve seen a huge amount of work happening behind the scenes, with many experts offering their time and knowledge to tackle different aspects of the challenge. Communicated clearly, this information plays a central role in supporting operational responders and decision makers.
No single organisation holds all the scientific knowledge and skills needed during a complex environmental incident like this.

That is why the science committee draws on expertise from across government, environmental regulators, public health specialists and marine scientists. I am working closely with colleagues on the committee from local groups, government organisations including Natural England, Cefas, the Marine Management Organisation, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency and UKHSA, as well as academic experts from the universities of Newcastle, Portsmouth and Lancaster, bringing together a broad range of scientific disciplines.

This collaborative approach ensures that decisions are informed by the best available evidence, whether the issue is wildlife conservation, fisheries, public health, or marine pollution. It also means that advice provided to the local authorities and others leading the response is consistent, actionable and reliable.

Day to day, scientists from the Environment Agency and partner organisations work together on a wide range of environmental challenges, from water quality and flood risk to emerging pollutants and incident response.
By combining evidence, expert judgement and collaboration across organisations, we can better understand environmental risks, make informed decisions and help protect people and the environment.

Science does not necessarily remove uncertainty, but it gives us the best possible foundation for making balanced and informed decisions when it matters most. I am grateful to everyone helping to make this a reality in the North East.

title: Coverage of plans to strengthen mayoral powers over planning decisions

content.content: Following an announcement earlier this week, there has been widespread national coverage of the government’s plans to give regional mayors greater powers over major planning decisions, as part of efforts to boost housebuilding, unlock growth and deliver devolution.

The measures allow mayors to call in and determine significant planning applications, including housing developments of more than 150 homes, commercial schemes over 15,000 square metres and buildings over ten storeys tall.

The Sunday Times first reported the plans following an interview with the Prime Minister, who said the reforms would help local leaders drive growth and deliver the homes their areas need. The paper reported that the proposals have the backing of several regional mayors and highlighted comments from Andy Burnham, who said the aim was to give local areas “more grip over the most fundamental thing their areas need, which is homes that people can afford”.

The government has been clear that any mayoral interventions would still need to be consistent with planning law and local development plans. The reforms are intended to help local leaders unlock development, accelerate housing delivery and support growth across England.

Broadcast coverage on BBC News and ITV News reported that the reforms form part of the government’s wider devolution agenda and could also give mayors greater influence over infrastructure funding and economic development in their areas.
Both broadcasters ran comments from Housing and Planning Minister Matthew Pennycook, who said:

“At the end of the day, it's local leaders who know best how to realise the full economic potential of their areas. These new powers will help them to do that and ensure we get good growth in every postcode.”

Coverage then appeared across a range of national newspapers and broadcasters. The Guardian, Mirror, i Paper, Independent, Metro, Sun and Telegraph all reported on the proposals, explaining that mayors would receive powers similar to those already held by the Mayor of London.

Several reports noted that the government believes the reforms will help speed up development, support economic growth and unblock housing schemes that have become stalled in the planning system. The Telegraph reported that the measures could help unlock thousands of homes currently delayed or blocked.

title: Coverage of first wave of funding from the Social and Affordable Homes Programme

content.content: There has been widespread national, regional, broadcast and social media coverage of the government’s announcement of the first wave of funding from the £39 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme.

The government confirmed almost £10 billion will be allocated to councils, housing associations and other providers outside London to support the delivery of more than 70,000 new social and affordable homes, with the majority of homes available for social rent.

The announcement forms part of the government’s wider commitment to deliver 300,000 social and affordable homes and help families stuck in temporary accommodation or on housing waiting lists access a safe and secure home.
National newspapers

The i Paper prominently splashed the announcement on its front page, reporting that more than 70,000 homes will be built to help tackle the housing crisis and reduce the growing costs of temporary accommodation for councils. The paper carried an interview with the Housing Secretary, highlighting the government’s focus on council and social housing and describing the announcement as a significant shift towards delivering more genuinely affordable homes.
The Mirror also reported positively on the announcement, focusing on the first £10 billion allocation and the Prime Minister’s call to “build this country out of a housing crisis”.
The Independent described the investment as a “council house comeback” and reported on the government’s ambition to increase the supply of social and council housing.
The Times covered the regional allocations, reporting that London will receive more than £6 billion and highlighting substantial funding for mayoral areas across England.

The Financial Times and Guardian highlighted support from the housing sector. The Financial Times carried comments from National Housing Federation chief executive Kate Henderson, who described the allocation as “a major vote of confidence in not-for-profit housing associations and in the vital and distinct role they play”, and the Guardian carried an exclusive SoS quote that she ‘knows firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.’.
National broadcast

The announcement featured prominently across national broadcasters, including BBC News, BBC Breakfast, BBC Radio 4 Today, Sky News, ITV News, ITV Good Morning Britain, Times Radio and LBC, following a series of ministerial interviews.

BBC News reported that more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be delivered through the first allocations from the programme. Coverage focused on the scale of housing need, with contributions from families living in temporary accommodation and housing charities calling for further action to increase supply.

The report included comments from the Secretary of State, who said councils are eager to build more homes and that the government is committed to supporting them to do so. The BBC News package ran across online, socials, broadcast as well as Newscast.

ITV News similarly reported that funding would support the delivery of over 70,000 homes across England, with a large proportion available for social rent. The coverage highlighted the role of councils, housing associations and strategic partners in delivering homes at scale, while also discussing wider challenges facing the housing sector.

Across broadcasters, there was significant focus on homelessness, housing waiting lists and the need for more social housing, alongside discussion of how the funding could help reduce the number of families living in temporary accommodation.
Social media

Housing campaigner Kwajo Tweneboa published an interview with Deputy Prime Minister and Housing Secretary Angela Rayner on Instagram discussing the government’s housing programme and the importance of increasing social and council housebuilding.

In the interview, the Secretary of State described the investment as part of the government’s determination to tackle the housing crisis, reduce the number of children growing up in temporary accommodation and increase the supply of social and council homes.

Across Instagram and TikTok, ITV News posted two clips from interviews with Housing and Planning Minister Matthew Pennycook following the Social and Affordable Homes Programme announcement. The videos focused on government plans to deliver more than 70,000 social and affordable homes, with 60% for social rent, while responding to questions on eligibility for social housing and whether Labour remains on track to meet its target of building 1.5 million homes over the Parliament.
Regional coverage
There has been extensive positive regional coverage focusing on local funding allocations and the number of homes expected to be delivered.

The Manchester Evening News and BBC North West highlighted almost £1 billion of funding for the North West, including more than £529 million for Greater Manchester to support around 4,000 social and affordable homes. Coverage featured comments from Housing and Planning Minister Matthew Pennycook and regional leaders on tackling homelessness and increasing housing supply.
The Liverpool Echo reported on funding for the Liverpool City Region, where around 3,100 homes are expected to be delivered through the programme.

In London, BBC London dedicated significant coverage to the capital’s £6 billion allocation. The programme featured interviews with Minister Pennycook and Mayor Sadiq Khan, alongside residents and housing campaigners, focusing on the need for more affordable housing and the challenge of meeting demand.

Elsewhere, outlets including the Evening Standard, Telegraph & Argus, Express & Star, Yorkshire Live, Chronicle Live and other regional titles covered local funding allocations and reported supportive comments from regional mayors and housing stakeholders.

Across regional media, coverage largely focused on the number of homes expected to be delivered in each area, the benefits for families on housing waiting lists, and the role the funding could play in addressing local housing pressures.
Secretary of State Angela Rayner said:
“Families can’t be left raising children without a place to call home, and none of us should spend years waiting for somewhere safe and affordable to live.
“I know how important fixing this is – because I’ve been there. A safe and secure home was the foundation for a better life - I couldn’t have got to where I have today without it.

“That’s why the Prime Minister and I are doing everything we can to get councils building once again – it’s fundamental to turning the housing crisis around, helping families out of temporary accommodation and into a secure home.”

title: Building technology with purpose: how we developed Business Finder

content.content: Export support

As the department for economic growth, the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) supports businesses to invest, grow and export. The new Digital Exports Support team is a community of advisers who help businesses to export their products and services. To do this they need to identify businesses of all sizes and across all sectors across England that need support. The support can be anything from spotting an opportunity for export, developing an export plan, unblocking trade barriers and introducing the business to other services.
One of their biggest challenges is knowing which businesses are most likely to benefit from support, and how to find them consistently across different sectors and regions.

With the establishment of the Digital Exports Support team, there was an opportunity to explore more data-led ways to find businesses digitally. This has reduced the burden of time spent travelling and attending costly events. Data was available to support this task, but it was spread across BIST, HMRC and Companies House. We realised we could take advantage of new developments in AI technology to bring this data together and uncover companies that need support.

This led us on a journey that highlights the benefits of working in a digital role in the public sector. It meant being close to users, building technology that solved real problems and supported UK businesses, and having the opportunity to unlock value from administrative data.
Finding businesses in need of export support

Our goal was to turn data into a practical tool that could help advisers identify, prioritise and act on potential export leads. We have built upon an experiment run by our Data Science team a few years earlier, and called the tool Business Finder.

The tool was built on an algorithm that uses openly-available data about companies and their financial and export activity to predict how likely they are to export successfully. It is a machine learning model that is trained on historical data. Training involves improving the model’s accuracy by comparing its predictions against reality over thousands of iterations. Once the model is trained, it can look at information about a business and produce an ‘Export Propensity’ score. This reflects the business’s likelihood of exporting in the next 6 months. Companies are ranked on the Business Finder tool in order of their score.
By bringing together data from BIST, HMRC and Companies House, we turned the idea from a promising model to a practical product that would unlock the data’s value.
One of the values we champion in BIST Digital, Data and Technology (DDaT) is user centred design. So, we made sure to stay close to trade advisers throughout the development process.

For Business Finder to be useful, advisers needed to understand the export propensity score in context. A range of filters were added to the tool that allowed managers to assign leads to their teams, including:
Bringing these data points together gave advisers a fuller picture of each business and empowered managers to curate a prioritised list.
Testing and iterating the product
Within 12 weeks we had our beta product: a ranked, searchable list of potential export leads that teams could use in their day-to-day work.

10 users who trained to use the tool were asked to give feedback within it. This included providing their personal score for a business alongside a rationale for that score. Feedback was also collected through focus groups, forms, and interviews.
Recalibrating the algorithm

Testing revealed that to be valuable the tool needed to surface trustworthy leads. When early feedback uncovered glitches in how the businesses were ranking, the team used adviser insight to recalibrate the model.

Initially, the reference point for company data was fixed to a date 8 years ago. A huge financial variation was possible over this 8-year gap, especially with the pandemic. This reference point was improved to be set at 36 months prior. Financial information would now be closer to the current reality of the company.

This update improved the relevance of the leads being suggested. User feedback increasingly supported the rankings produced by the model. The recommended businesses were now more relevant and represented more viable opportunities to contact for support. This gave the team greater confidence that Business Finder was surfacing businesses with genuine export potential.

Confidence in our tools’ outputs is key to our work here at BIST. Our products have value when they are used to improve outcomes for the businesses we support. They are not used until they are trusted.
Impact

This new ability to direct the adviser focus on specific sectors, areas and company types is a game-changer. In the past, finding leads was inconsistent, time-consuming and often sourced organically through word of mouth, personal contacts and networks.

By bringing together data from BIST, HMRC and Companies House we have empowered advisers with a data-led view of businesses that may be ready for support. This allows advisers to spend less time identifying and verifying leads and more time providing valuable support to the businesses most likely to benefit.

Having access to a list of businesses sorted by likelihood of exporting can speed up the lead generation process. It also broadens the reach and reveals opportunities that may not have been found through existing relationships.
Learning from real use of Business Finder
It was our user-led approach to developing the tool that built advisers' confidence and trust in it. This encouraged them to use it and help us to improve it.

Business Finder is still being shaped by how advisers use it in practice. With complex data products it can be difficult to understand how people use the product. With so many variables, use cases and ways of working, it is hard to learn from a prototype using mock data alone. The model is only one part of the service, and the way leads are filtered, interpreted and acted on is just as important as the score itself.

We learned from realistic user engagement with the small beta test group. These early testers used the product in real life scenarios, which gave more reliable feedback than hypothetical testing. The testing gave our team evidence about where the model was working well and how it should evolve.
Within the first 2 weeks we spotted repeating patterns in the feedback we gathered. These are now shaping future iterations of the design.
At BIST we build products that solve real problems. To help the UK economy grow, we combine data, user insight and delivery expertise together.

Updating, refining and improving products based on how they are actually used is an important foundation to how we deliver digital products. By improving the product based on real feedback, we can make it more useful for advisers, and ultimately for the businesses they support.
Conclusion

By building this product we have made valuable data useable so that advisers can effectively find and support potential exporters more consistently. Using innovative AI technology, we’re now reaching UK businesses who would have not been discovered before, and supporting them to grow and adapt in a challenging business landscape.

title: First year as a Marine Surveyor after a career at sea

content.content: After a career at sea as a deck officer, Robert Taylor joined the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) as a Marine Surveyor.

How did his first year with us go? From training and travel to last-minute changes of plans, Rob reflects on what he’s learned, the support he’s received from his colleagues, the places he’s visited, and what you can expect when joining the MCA as a marine surveyor.

It takes a full year for a new entrant to qualify as a marine surveyor. That may seem a long time, but there is good reason. In addition to shadowing surveyors as they carried out their survey and inspection work, I had 13 short courses to attend, requiring travel to offices, harbours, and boatyards in Southampton, Belfast, Lowestoft, and Lisbon.

The scope of the job is unusually wide, and the work must be done to a consistent, high standard. I came to the MCA from a seafaring background, as a deck officer having sailed on a variety of ship types. This meant that, while my knowledge of navigation and ship’s equipment was up to speed, I had a great deal to learn about the likes of ship construction, repair, fire protection and engineering.
Working in Aberdeen

From the third floor of Marine House, within Aberdeen harbour limits, the Marine Office windows give a panoramic view of the North Harbour. Ships can be seen coming and going; often, a glance from the window saves looking online to check where a given vessel has berthed. For vessel visits within the harbour, it is often possible to walk. This is where I spent much of my first year (two to three days every week when I wasn’t on a course) as I got up to speed with the MCA working practices and the instructions to surveyors – the internal guidance documents that are so important for doing the job well.

The work didn’t end at the office door or the harbour limits. Aberdeen Marine Office sees to a dramatic and beautiful part of Scotland; from the red sandstone harbours in Angus, through Moray, the Caithness coast, across the Pentland Firth to the Orkney and the Fair Isle Gap to Shetland, and down the scenic west coast as far as Lochinver. The role offers the opportunity to work across some of the most remote mainland and island communities. Surveyors travel to where vessels are based, with visits sometimes involving a week-long stay to ensure effective service delivery.

In my first year, I spent a week on Orkney surveying small fishing vessels and carrying out an audit for a ferry company, and I’ve spent a week in Caithness this May. I got to know the roads between Peterhead, Fraserburgh, Macduff, and Aberdeen by heart.

Some visits were planned months in advance; the business services team liaises with companies and fishers to find a suitable date, and the work is apportioned among the surveyors based on workload and experience. Other visits were, by their nature, spur-of-the-moment, reacting to an incident, or to carry out a port state control inspection. This demands flexibility and adaptability from both the organisation and the surveyor. I learned to keep my bag packed and be ready to change plans at the drop of a hat. This is not a 9am to 5pm job. But the flexibility works both ways; overtime can be taken as time off in lieu, and whenever possible duty shifts can be swapped with colleagues to fit with holiday plans.
Training

The training required for each survey type is laid out in a structured training plan: how many surveys must be witnessed, how many must be carried out under supervision, and an assessment of theoretical knowledge and relevant legislation. From day one, I found myself attending International Safety Management (ISM) audits, International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) verifications, Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) inspections, and re-validations of Safety Equipment Certificates and Certificate of Survey of Vessel Standing by Offshore Installations.  In addition to this merchant vessel work, a great deal of my time was spent on fishing vessels; everything from under-15m open-decked wooden hulls to 23m long trawlers and 70m long pelagic boats.
Inspecting fishing vessels

Scotland’s east coast is a fishing powerhouse; around 78% of the total fish landed in the UK in 2024 came ashore at either Peterhead or Lerwick. Consequently, a significant part of Aberdeen Marine Office’s workload relates to the fishing fleet. The legislation regulating this enormous industry, both international and UK-specific, must be well understood and consistently applied by the surveyor. In addition to understanding the legal side of things, it is important that the surveyor appreciates the unique culture and heritage of the communities that these vessels support. Immediately on finishing my training year, I found myself attending fishing vessels that had gone aground or lost engine power, speaking with skippers and crews to understand what had happened and to identify any lessons that could help improve safety. On some days I’d arrive at a harbour to carry out a routine job – an out-of-water inspection of a fishing vessel, for example – and take the opportunity to speak with fishers about their vessels, operations and any safety concerns they might have. These conversations often provide valuable insights and help build the relationships needed to promote a strong safety culture across the industry. No two days are ever the same.
Learning and development

Having worked in the maritime sector for 15 years, being in and around vessels felt comfortable for me from the get-go. Learning MCA procedures and the ins and outs of the role have been my biggest learning opportunity, but working in an office filled with experienced surveyors and carrying out ship visits with them, gave me an excellent practical learning environment. The technical manager, business manager and my line manager have worked together to ensure I saw the right kind of survey work during my training year. Now I’ve qualified, they continue to keep an eye on my workload and development.

My advice to anyone interested in becoming a surveyor is to jump in with both feet. It's a professional role with a lot of responsibility, so there's naturally a lot to learn, but that also brings a greater sense of pride. Your colleagues – chief engineers, master mariners and naval architects – are only ever a phone call or an email away, and I still value that support network today. From my experience, they are always happy to give their knowledge and advice.

description: Rob reflects on a year working for the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as a surveyor.

title: Tackling antimicrobial resistance: what seven years of global work has taught us

content.content: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is often called the “silent pandemic”. It affects how well medicines work, not just in hospitals, but in farming, food production and the environment. When antibiotics stop working, infections become harder to treat, food systems become more vulnerable, and risks to human and animal health increase.

Over the past seven years, our team at the UK FAO Reference Centre for Antimicrobial Resistance, has worked with partners across Africa and Asia to help tackle this growing challenge. Supported by the Fleming Fund, we focused on a simple idea: if countries can reliably detect, understand and respond to antimicrobial resistance, they can take action to reduce it.

A defining feature of this work has been close partnership with FAO, whose in-country presence, regional networks, and understanding of national priorities ensured that activities were well aligned, locally relevant, and embedded within existing systems. This enabled more effective delivery and stronger, more sustainable outcomes across the programme.
Building the foundations: better data, stronger systems

A key part of the work has been strengthening laboratory capacity. In many countries, laboratories faced challenges such as limited equipment, supply issues, and inconsistent testing methods. Through training, mentoring, and quality assurance schemes, we supported laboratories to improve their ability to identify resistant bacteria and produce reliable data.
This matters because good decisions depend on good data. Without knowing where and how resistance is occurring, it is difficult to target interventions or measure progress.
Working with people: from training to global networks

Alongside technical work, we invested heavily in people. Over the course of the programme, we delivered training, hosted scientists in UK laboratories, and supported a growing international community of practice.

Today, that community connects professionals from across the world, creating space for knowledge sharing and collaboration beyond individual projects. This has been essential for building confidence, sharing solutions, and sustaining progress across sectors.
Generating evidence to guide action

We also worked with partners on collaborative research to fill important evidence gaps. For example, studies on antimicrobial resistance in poultry systems and aquatic environments have provided new insights into how resistance spreads in food production systems.
These kinds of studies help translate science into policy, supporting countries to shape surveillance systems, national action plans, and regulatory approaches.
What we have learned
Looking back over seven years, some clear lessons stand out.
First, long-term partnerships matter. Countries that we worked with over multiple years showed the greatest progress, particularly in laboratory quality and surveillance systems.
Second, hands-on support makes a difference. While remote training can be useful, in-country mentoring and practical experience were far more effective in building lasting capability.
Third, strong systems are just as important as individual skills. Laboratory improvements cannot be sustained without reliable supply chains, stable infrastructure, and ongoing investment.
A lasting legacy
Building on seven years of partnership and capacity strengthening, laboratories are better equipped, professionals are better connected, and countries are better positioned to respond to AMR.
The Fleming Fund programme formally concluded in March 2026, but the work of the UK FAO Reference Centre for Antimicrobial Resistance continues.

Looking ahead, we will continue to support countries to strengthen surveillance, translate data into action, and deepen One Health collaboration, ensuring that the progress made evolves into sustained, long-term impact.

title: Coverage of national drive to end rough sleeping

content.content: There is extensive national coverage across print, broadcast and digital platforms of the department’s announcement that everyone sleeping rough in England will be offered a route off the streets this winter, backed by a £442 million package.

Following an interview with the Secretary of State, the I Paper led on its front page that this marks the first phase of the PM’s ambitious Housing First strategy to end rough sleeping and reflected that “getting everyone in” is the “start of a process” to end rough sleeping.

Other outlets including The Daily Mirror, ITV News, The Guardian, The Financial Times, LBC, BBC News, The Independent, GB News, The Daily Telegraph, Big Issue and The Sun also report on the announcement prominently – pointing to the Prime Minister’s plans to convene a ‘first of its kind’ national summit on ending rough sleeping in the autumn, bringing together leaders from business, finance, health and faith communities to ask how they can all play a role. Coverage also reflects on Greater Manchester’s A Bed Every Night covid-era scheme that aims to provide support to anyone sleeping rough in the region.
Ministers also wrote directly for various outlets, sharing the reasons why this mission is so important:

Numerous regional outlets have reflected funding allocations for their local areas, including Harrogate Advertiser, Exeter Today, Derbyshire Live, Milton Keynes Citizen, Newark Advertiser, Manchester Evening News and Lancaster Guardian, as well as many regional radio stations.
Charities and homelessness projects have also responded to the announcement, including:
Matt Downie, Chief Executive of Crisis, said:

“Today’s announcement represents a clear statement that in the 21st century, we will not tolerate a situation where people are having to bed down on our streets. It puts us on the path to an historic milestone: the end of rough sleeping in England.

“Being forced to sleep rough puts people at increased risk of serious illness, violence, and abuse. The average age of death for people experiencing homelessness is 45 for men and 43 for women. So getting people off the streets and onto the path to a settled, secure home will save lives.
“In the long-term, rough sleeping can only be solved with the provision of safe, affordable homes, so we really welcome the funding to provide more settled homes.

“Where access to a home isn't possible straight away, providing good quality accommodation with a clear plan to support people into settled housing is a vital first step. We stand ready to help the Prime Minister in delivering this vital intervention ahead of Christmas, starting with this Autumn’s summit that will bring together civil society, businesses and faith leaders to help deliver on the Government’s vision of a country without rough sleeping.”
Dr Emma Haddad, Chief Executive of St Mungo's, said:

“Today’s announcement marks a pivotal moment for the thousands of people experiencing rough sleeping: an acknowledgement from the highest level of political leadership that rough sleeping should not exist, and a decisive step forward to end it once and for all.

In 21st Century Britain, nobody should be forced to sleep on the streets. We have long been calling for urgent and decisive action to end rough sleeping, and we wholeheartedly welcome Andy Burnham’s commitment to offer a route off the streets for everyone sleeping rough by Christmas, with a longer term, sustainable, housing-led programme developed alongside. It is exactly the kind of intervention needed to save lives, and to begin turning the tide on record levels of rough sleeping.

Every day, we see the devastating impact rough sleeping has on people’s health, safety and hope for the future. It deepens trauma, negatively impacts mental and physical health, and makes it even harder to access support. Housing is key, but housing alone will not be enough. A roof over somebody’s head provides immediate safety, but lasting recovery requires intensive, person-centred, joined-up support.

That today’s announcement provides both a commitment to get people off the streets quickly, as well as the tailored support needed to help them stay off them for good, is exactly the right approach. We stand ready to work with the Government, this winter and beyond, to make that ambition a reality.”
Lord Bird, the co-founder of the Big Issue and a crossbench peer, said:
“COVID proved that when we decide rough sleeping is unacceptable, we can act and get people in off the streets. This Christmas commitment is a welcome return to that spirit.

“But it’s important that people are not just brought in from the cold for a few weeks, only to be sent back out again. To that end, I’m encouraged to see the Prime Minister is allocating millions in tried-and-tested localised solutions that offer wraparound support for long-term rough sleepers. Countless projects and pilots demonstrated this approach works, only to be suffocated by the underinvestment and short-termist mindset of the previous government.

“In all my years at the Big Issue, I’ve never met a rough sleeper whose only problem was homelessness. Rough sleeping is a destination after years of untreated issues, like mental health problems, abuse and substance addictions – none of which simply vanishes when you get a roof over someone’s head. Instead we must start treating the causes of homelessness and begin the process of getting people back into society.”
Seyi Obakin, Chief Executive of youth homelessness charity Centrepoint, said:

“It is brilliant to see the Prime Minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping backed by a serious commitment of funding. We know how to eradicate street homelessness, not just for winter but with long-term investment in the systems and solutions that will ensure people aren’t forced to return to the streets and newly homeless people are prevented from ending up on the streets. What has been missing for too long is the will to do it at the scale and consistency required. With sustained funding and a clear plan that includes frontline delivery practitioners, this commitment can turn that ambition into reality and ensure all young people have the solid foundations of a home from which to build a future.”
Rick Henderson, CEO of Homeless Link, the national membership body for frontline homelessness organisations, comments:

“The Government’s commitment to a national drive to end rough sleeping, backed by clear action and additional funding is extremely welcome. We are pleased that the need for both emergency off the street provision and investment in practical support has been recognised, and that there is an understanding that this must move towards long term accommodation and support if we are to truly end rough sleeping for good.

“It is extremely encouraging to see the critical role of the voluntary and community fully acknowledged. We are delighted to see that the Ending Homelessness in Community Fund will receive additional funding to support the vital work of smaller and medium sized organisations across England, as well as the commitment to collaborative conversation with the VCS in shaping this work. We look forward to working with the Government to move towards a homelessness system that’s rooted in prevention and support, and making ending rough sleeping a reality.”
Liz Rutherfoord, Chief Executive, Single Homeless Project:

"This announcement is a huge step forward in ending rough sleeping for everyone - including the thousands of women in England who's rough sleeping has previously been overlooked by successive governments. Women's rough sleeping is hidden, transient and intermittent, and almost always interlinked with violence and abuse. The Prime Minister's new funding announcement and guidance to local authorities is unprecedented, as it finally puts a spotlight on women's rough sleeping, and urges local authorities to ensure that their efforts to get everyone in don't leave women behind. Linking the commitment to end rough sleeping to the pledge to halve VAWG is essential - one is not possible without the other."
Nahar Choudhury, chief executive of Solace, said:
“This is a positive step towards fulfilling government commitments to end rough sleeping and halve violence against women and girls.

“We welcome the government’s recognition that women’s experiences of rough sleeping are fundamentally different from men’s and that women are under-represented in official statistics. This guidance highlights the need for local authorities to respond in a way that reflects women’s reality.

“Violence against women and girls is a cause and consequence of having nowhere safe to stay. Encouraging the use of women-only accommodation, alongside trauma-informed support, ensures survivors of violence and abuse are not subjected to further harm.”

title: Water Quality and Moorings Survey: life, data and science at sea

content.content: Monitoring our UK Marine waters

Monitoring marine pollution in UK waters is essential for understanding how coastal and offshore ecosystems are changing, where pressures are emerging, and whether management actions are helping seas recover. Long-term, high-quality observations of nutrients, chlorophyll, dissolved oxygen, suspended sediments, contaminants, underwater noise and biological communities provide the evidence base needed to assess environmental status and detect change over time. These data underpin the UK’s national marine assessments, including reporting for OSPAR and the UK Marine Strategy, helping to track progress towards Good Environmental Status and inform decisions that protect the health, productivity and resilience of our seas.

Cefas delivers much of this evidence through regular surveys on the RV Cefas Endeavour, where scientists collect seawater samples, deploy and recover autonomous instruments, and gather continuous measurements from ship-based systems. Once ashore, samples and sensor records are quality assured, analysed and combined to support national monitoring and assessment. To spotlight how this important work is done, a member of the Cefas communications team, Fiona Vogt, joined the quarterly Water Quality and Moorings Survey, following the scientists and crew as they collected the data that informs marine assessment, policy and management, to highlight the impact of this science in strengthening food security and supporting the marine environment and economic growth.
Day 0 – from Lowestoft Harbour to the North Sea

Day 0 began alongside the quay in Lowestoft, with the RV Cefas Endeavour being prepared for departure and the survey team making final checks before heading to sea. Scientific equipment was being readied, sampling plans were reviewed, and the team were working through the practical steps needed to ensure the first stations could be completed safely and efficiently once the vessel left harbour. For the communications team, joining the survey meant being embedded in this busy preparation phase: observing how the science is organised, speaking with the survey leads and crew, and beginning to capture the people, equipment and planning behind the monitoring programme.

Before sailing, the communications role was also to understand the rhythm of life onboard: where filming and photography could take place safely, when scientists and crew would be available to talk, and how to document the work without interrupting operations. The vessel is both a workplace and a home during survey, and so the first day included familiarisation with the ship, safety procedures, and the working areas where water sampling, mooring preparation and deck operations would take place. Cefas Endeavour is operated and maintained by AW Ship Management (AWSM) and is also home to their crew, who work closely with Cefas scientists, providing essential support.
The plan was to capture the journey from ship to assessment: how samples are collected, instruments deployed and recovered, and observations turned into evidence for the UK marine environment.

Once preparations were complete, the Cefas Endeavour left Lowestoft harbour and headed out towards the first survey stations in the North Sea. The programme runs around the clock, with 12-hour day and night shifts covering water sampling, instrument checks, deployments and recoveries.

The communications work kept pace with the survey, documenting activity as it happened. After watching from the back deck as we left Lowestoft harbour and sailed under the bridge, I was happy to have an early night, to make sure we were ready for an early start.
Day 0 Linked In Post
Day 1 at sea – monitoring begins in the southern North Sea

Day 1 began early, with calm seas, clear skies and the survey already well underway. The scientific programme had begun overnight, with hourly seawater sampling and continuous FerryBox measurements recording changing conditions as the vessel moved between stations.

At 03:00, the team had deployed a SmartBuoy fitted with near real-time water quality sensors. These SmarBuoy moorings provide long-term observations of temperature, oxygen, turbidity, chlorophyll and other indicators, helping scientists track environmental change and pollution pressures over time.
See the SmartBuoy webpage for more information and latest data.
At 6.00am, I met Izzy Lake, the Survey Lead, and Elise Brabben, the deputy Survey Lead on the bridge to talk through the day’s schedule and how best to share the importance of the work.

Throughout Friday, we stopped at stations across the Thames River plume region, retrieving and deploying equipment including SmartBuoys, Noise Seabed Landers, the CTD (Conductivity Temperature Depth) rosette, a Secchi disk and zooplankton ringnet. Seawater samples were also collected for nutrients, chlorophyll-a, suspended particulate matter, oxygen, salinity, Coloured Dissolved Organic Matter (CDOM) and phytoplankton. Together, these measurements show how nutrients, suspended sediments, oxygen levels and plankton communities are changing across the survey area. Environmental DNA, or eDNA, was also collected to support biodiversity monitoring method validation.

Noise Seabed Landers record underwater sound at the seabed using hydrophones, contributing to national assessments of underwater noise as a pressure on the marine environment. The UK has a marine noise threshold, and we report what is recorded, which ranges from boat traffic to harbour porpoises.  On this survey, one lander was deployed at Warp in the Thames Estuary.

Retrievals and deployments rely on close coordination between Cefas scientists and the AWSM crew. The work required careful planning, clear communication and suitable conditions, especially when heavy moorings, buoys and sensor frames were moved safely over the side of the vessel.

On the back deck, Cefas colleagues prepared SmartBuoys, Noise Seabed Landers and other moored instruments for deployment. Their work combines practical engineering skill, sensor knowledge and careful safety procedures, much of it prepared in the workshop before the vessel leaves port. The onboard Cefas engineer, kept the scientific systems running, troubleshooting alarms, power issues and data streams.

The water sampling team kept monitoring running throughout the survey. They deployed the CTD rosette, took Secchi disk and ocean colour readings, and processed samples. The CTD records conductivity, temperature to assess seawater clarity, and depth through the water column, while taking and preserving the seawater samples from the Niskin bottles from specific depths for laboratory analysis, building a picture of water column structure, light availability, nutrients and plankton communities.

As I reached the end of the first day, I was struck by the breadth of methods, skills and knowledge needed from scientists and crew to collect the evidence behind behind national marine assessments, from water quality and biodiversity to climate change.
After a full day of sampling, deployments, filming and conversations with the team, sea air, shift work and hearty food from the ship’s chefs made an early night very welcome.
Day 1 LinkedIn Post
Day 2 at sea – instruments, indicators and long-term evidence

Day Two continued across OSPAR Commission assessment areas in the southern North Sea, with the team collecting the physical, chemical and biological data needed to assess marine environmental status.At Dowsing station, the CTD rosette was deployed to collect conductivity, temperature and depth profiles, alongside seawater samples from Niskin bottles. These data support eutrophication assessments and pelagic food web monitoring by linking nutrients, chlorophyll, dissolved oxygen, plankton communities and other indicators to ecosystem condition.A Noise Seabed Lander was also deployed at Dowsing, protected by two guard buoys during its four-month deployment. The lander records underwater sound at the seabed and carries an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler and CTD profiler, helping build a clearer picture of acoustic pressure and local water column conditions.The Dowsing Waverider was serviced because the battery in the existing deployment was running low. A replacement mooring and Waverider buoy were deployed to maintain the long-term wave record used for flood forecasting and marine monitoring. Waveriders also measure sea surface temperature, contributing to evidence on changing seas and recent marine heatwaves.

Together, these instruments form part of a long-running national programme that combines ship-based sampling with in-situ moorings to provide consistent data for UK and regional assessments. Maintaining this evidence base over many years is essential for detecting change, understanding pressures and assessing progress towards Good Environmental Status.The survey depends on a multidisciplinary team, including biogeochemists, engineers, analytical chemists, plankton specialists, data scientists, modellers, project managers, scientific survey leads and vessel crew. The AWSM crew are central to keeping the ship running safely and efficiently, enabling sampling, deployments and recoveries across a demanding programme.
Day 2 LinkedIn Post
Day 3 at sea – completing the survey and bringing the evidence home

By Day 3, the moorings section of the survey was complete, and the Cefas Endeavour was on the home stretch back towards Lowestoft. The focus shifted to completing the remaining transects (taking samples along a consistent route) across the Humber Plume and Wash assessment areas, where the team continued collecting seawater samples and supporting measurements needed for water quality assessment.

Sampling continued as the vessel moved between stations, adding to the survey record for nutrients, chlorophyll-a, suspended sediments, dissolved oxygen, plankton and other indicators. These measurements build a spatial picture of water quality across coastal and offshore assessment areas.

As the ship made its way back to Lowestoft, the scientific programme began to wind down. Metadata were checked and quality assured, samples were organised for return to the laboratory, and work areas were cleaned and packed down safely. This final stage is an important part of the survey process: good data depend not only on collecting the right samples, but also on accurate records, careful handling and consistent quality control.

Once ashore, the samples were taken to the Lowestoft laboratory for analysis. The resulting data feed into UK Marine Strategy and OSPAR assessments, both of which are reported on six-year cycles, helping determine whether UK seas are achieving or maintaining Good Environmental Status. Assessments draw on temporal trends as well as the latest observations, which means that each survey adds an important new layer of evidence while building on the historical record. Regularly updated data are therefore essential for every assessment cycle, ensuring changes in nutrients, chlorophyll, oxygen, sediments and plankton can be tracked consistently over time. The data also support calibration and validation of SmartBuoy, CTD, FerryBox and ship-based biogeochemical sensors, keeping year-round observations accurate and comparable.

The RV Cefas Endeavour spends more than 300 days at sea each year and is a strategic monitoring asset for the UK government. Surveys like this bring together ship-based sampling, autonomous moorings, sensor systems and laboratory analysis to provide the long-term evidence needed to understand environmental change and support healthy, productive seas.
Find out more about integrated marine monitoring to support UK and international ambitions to support healthy and productive seas in this blog.
Day 3 LinkedIn Post
Final thoughts

Spending time on board showed me how much preparation, coordination and technical work goes into each monitoring survey. Long before the vessel leaves port, equipment is prepared and tested, sampling plans are agreed, safety procedures are checked and teams work through the logistics needed to deliver a demanding programme at sea.These surveys depend on an integrated, multidisciplinary team. Scientists, engineers, technicians, analysts, data specialists, survey leads and vessel crew all bring different expertise, but the monitoring only works because those roles come together as one coordinated effort. From deck operations and sensor checks to sample processing and laboratory analysis, each stage contributes to the evidence chain that helps explain what is happening in UK waters.The Water Quality and Moorings Survey provides crucial evidence on nutrients, sediments, underwater noise, climate variability and wider ecosystem responses. This evidence supports national assessments, informs advice to Defra and the UK government, and helps ensure decisions about marine policy and management are based on robust, long-term observations. Ultimately, this monitoring is essential for protecting and restoring healthy, productive and resilient seas.

To find out more about how these data are used after the survey, read the Measuring UK Marine Water Quality story map, which explains how monitoring evidence is brought together for national assessments — from sample collection and laboratory analysis through to interpretation and reporting.
You can also read the most recent OSPAR eutrophication assessment for the North-East Atlantic, and the latest eutrophication assessment for the UK Marine Strategy .

title: Tackling the loneliness of leaving care

content.content: Clare Chamberlain, co-chair of the Independent Review into the Deaths of Care Leavers, shares what the review found, and why care leavers need more than a Personal Adviser to help them navigate life after care and thrive as adults.
Why I wanted to lead this review

When I heard about this review, I was immediately very interested in being selected to co-lead the work. I am a retired Director of Children’s Services and since the early days of my time as a senior leader, I have heard many, many times from groups of young care leavers who feel that we don’t understand, or meet, their wants and needs. The state is no substitute for family. This review of early deaths of young people who have left care has only reinforced that message.  Over the last few months, I have been working alongside the co-lead for the review, Ashley John-Baptiste, a young man in his 30s with care experience and skill as a working broadcast journalist. We have visited local authorities and spoken to professionals and families who knew the young person who had died. There is 40 years between Ashley and myself, and we have had different life experiences, but we both felt that this combination worked well to provide alternative perspectives about what we found.
Loneliness, instability and the loss of trust

We heard of extreme vulnerability, of acute loneliness, and of young people who really had no trusted adult to help them deal with enormous difficulties they faced as older teenagers moving into their early twenties. These young people had experienced abuse, turbulent childhoods, instability, and trauma. Making sense of your childhood and thinking about your future as an adult is difficult enough for most of us, but without the solid support of family and friends, it can feel overwhelming.
When support falls away at 18

For me, the most important element of the review was a deepening of my understanding of just how difficult it is for young people to make that transition from child to adult. The experience of being in care is intense. As a child in care your health and wellbeing is closely monitored. Your emotional life is of concern to many, you are in meetings with adults who talk about you, who write copious notes about you, who make decisions about where you will live, who will look after you, where you will go to school, which members of your family you can see, and so on and so on. Then when you reach 18, so much of that falls away. What might seem a relief initially can soon turn into isolation and a sense of belonging to no-one. These were some of the most vulnerable of care leavers, those with the greatest needs and the task of helping them into adulthood is a complex one. We heard about young people who had experienced repeated rejection, who had suffered abuse as a child and who found difficulty in maintaining trusted relationships. We heard of young people who had made perilous journeys during their teenage years, alone in a foreign country without the security of family around them. We heard of young women who had lost the care of their children and who found this deeply traumatic, a huge loss for both parent and child.
Why we need more than a Personal Adviser

The workforce that we have supporting these young people mainly consists of Personal Advisers who help with practical tasks such as finding accommodation or helping with budget management. These are valued and trusted workers, but the overriding message I came away with is that we need a more sophisticated workforce to help young people transition into adulthood. We recommend the development of a wider team to support those Personal Advisers.  We need people who are very skilled; who can form a relationship of trust; who understand systemic practice and can help young people rebuild relationships with family; who have mental health expertise; and who can help young people reflect and come to terms with an unstable childhood and build confidence and emotional resilience to move into adulthood.

title: What is Salmonella and what can you do to avoid catching it?

content.content: Salmonella is the group of bacteria behind one of the most common types of food poisoning in the UK, and while for most people it means a few unpleasant days at home, for others it can lead to serious illness. With UKHSA currently helping to investigate a national outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK, we've answered some of the questions we're most commonly asked about this bacteria, the symptoms it causes, and how we track it.
What is Salmonella?
There are more than 2,500 different types of Salmonella. These bacteria live naturally in the guts of many domestic and wild animals, including chickens, cattle, pigs, hedgehogs, snakes and lizards.
The type most commonly responsible for making people ill in England is Salmonella Enteritidis.
Infection with Salmonella is known as salmonellosis.
How do you catch Salmonella?

Most people become infected through eating contaminated food. Salmonella can be found in foods such as eggs, chicken, pork and dairy products. Fruit and vegetables can also carry the bacteria if they've been in contact with livestock, manure or untreated water.
It is possible in rare cases to catch Salmonella from close contact with someone who has diarrhoea, or from contact with an unwell animal.

Good hygiene is vital. Wash your hands thoroughly after using the toilet and before preparing or handling food, wash utensils and chopping boards with hot water and cook food thoroughly. If you have symptoms yourself, avoid preparing food for others where you can.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms typically include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. These usually appear between 12 and 72 hours after infection, and illness typically lasts 4 to 7 days.

For most people, Salmonella causes a bout of gastroenteritis that clears up on its own. However, some people are at greater risk of more severe illness, including bloodstream infections, sepsis and, in rare cases, multi-organ failure.
How should it be treated?
Most people can manage Salmonella infection without needing to see a doctor.
The key things to do are:

There are also some things to avoid. Don't drink fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as these can make diarrhoea worse. Don't dilute baby formula, and don't give children under 12 medicines to stop diarrhoea, or give aspirin to children under 16.
A pharmacist can help if you or your child show signs of dehydration, are in a higher-risk group, or need something to stop diarrhoea for a few hours. They may suggest oral rehydration sachets.

You should call NHS 111 if you or your child has signs of dehydration that don't improve with rehydration sachets, can't keep fluids down, have bloody diarrhoea, or have diarrhoea that is not reducing in 3 days. If you're worried about a baby under 12 months, or a child under 5 shows signs of dehydration, call 111.
Call 999 or go to A&E for more serious symptoms, such as vomiting blood, a sudden severe headache or tummy ache, breathing difficulties, confusion, or blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin.
Is anyone more at risk, and what should they do differently?

While Salmonella causes a short, unpleasant illness for most people, some groups are more vulnerable to severe disease. This includes older people, pregnant women, young children and anyone with a weakened immune system such as those with cancer, kidney or liver failure, uncontrolled diabetes, steroid treatment or chemotherapy.

If you're in one of these groups, it's worth taking extra care, particularly around eggs. Eggs remain a healthy and safe part of the diet when properly handled and cooked, and you don't need to stop eating them. Ensure you use eggs with the British Lion mark or marked ‘Laid in Britain’. If you're eating out or buying food containing eggs that may not be British, it's safest to make sure any eggs you eat are thoroughly cooked. This means avoiding dishes such as soft boiled or poached eggs, fresh mayonnaise, mousses, soufflés and hollandaise sauce, unless you know the eggs used meet these assurance standards.
If you're in a vulnerable group and develop symptoms of Salmonella, it's worth seeking medical advice promptly rather than waiting to see if things improve on their own.
What does UKHSA do to monitor Salmonella and other gastro infections?
UKHSA's Gastrointestinal Infections, Food Safety and One Health (GIFSOH) division is responsible for monitoring cases of Salmonella and other gastrointestinal infections across the country.
This monitoring relies heavily on whole genome sequencing (WGS), a laboratory technique that allows scientists to compare the genetic fingerprint of bacteria from different cases.

When an unusual increase in cases is detected, UKHSA launches an outbreak investigation. This involves working closely with public health and food safety agencies across the UK and devolved administrations, as well as the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) and the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Investigators interview affected people to gather information about their symptoms and possible sources of infection, helping to build a picture of where contamination may have occurred and what control measures are needed.
Where can I find more information?
You can find wider UKHSA data on Salmonella on our website.

title: Services Week 2026 Wrap Up
authors: Steph Rowe, GDS Senior Events Manager

content.content: Thank you to everyone who made Services Week 2026 such a resounding success! It was inspiring to see the community come together to share, learn, and collaborate on improving public services.
This year, we saw an incredible turnout with around 4,000 attendees across 80 sessions, delivered by community members from over 30 different government departments.

Our most popular sessions included a talk from Lou Downe on "Bad services: how to fix services that don’t work", the User-Centred Design (UCD) team at Ofgem gave a popular demonstration on "Practical AI for User-Centred Design: Lessons from Experimenting with AI", and the Government Digital Service delivered an engaging session on "The Future of the Digital Service Standard".
Attendees from across the community told us that Services Week has helped them learn about other services, build connections and share practical approaches to service design.
They loved getting a clearer picture of different service areas and seeing how other teams put design principles into practice.
We are looking forward to hosting the event again next year with even more sessions to explore. We hope to be joined by many of you again, as well as lots of new faces.

We look forward to carrying this momentum forward, using the connections and collaborative spirit fostered over this week to continue supporting one another as we build and refine our community throughout the year ahead.
Join the Conversation

The energy doesn't have to end with Services Week! We encourage you to join the Services Week community on Slack using your government email address. It's the best place to stay connected with the service design community, share news, and ask questions.

title: Two Years On: My Reflections as Chief Regulator

content.content: Two years ago, the Environment Agency created the Chief Regulator's Group to provide strategic leadership for regulation. We’re helping create a more consistent, effective and proportionate regulatory system and strengthening the connection between strategy, policy and delivery.

Since then, my team and I have been driving that transformation. Meaningful change can take time. But we have made good strides forward as we move from improving individual parts of regulation towards creating a more joined-up and consistent regulatory system.
Improving transparency and access

For the first time, the public can read Compliance Assessment Report (CAR) forms without raising an information request. We've now shared thousands of water quality, waste, installations, and intensive pig and poultry forms on the Public Register Online.

At the same time, improved training and assurance have raised the quality of information available to the public on permit holder performance. We're building on this momentum, with more sectors to follow.
Faster, smarter permitting

Permitting is at the centre of our improvement work, and the Accelerated Permitting Transformation Programme is already delivering results. Queue times are at a three-year low, and the backlog has been reduced by over three-quarters. Enhanced validation has also cut determination times for complex applications by up to 100 days.

We’ve also introduced a Priority Tracked Service for complex multi-permit and Nationally Significant Infrastructure (NSIP) sites, currently supporting over 60 developments in housing, energy, infrastructure, mining and technology with strong customer feedback.

Our Regulatory Services Programme is powering our digital transformation by delivering smarter online journeys for our customers. Several types of permit applications are now fully digital, including Paper, Cardboard, and Plastic (PCP), Healthcare Waste (HCW), Waste Mattresses (WM), and Materials Recycling Facilities (MRF). Alongside this, an expansion of GOV.UK Pay for permit applications under £5,000 has saved a significant amount of processing time.
Driving forward sector improvements
We support responsible businesses to thrive sustainably while acting firmly when standards fall short.

Two priority areas have been water quality and waste crime. In March, we published our 10-point plan on waste crime to strengthen and accelerate action in this growing area of concern. It focuses on earlier intervention and stronger enforcement against poor performers, while tightening controls and accountability across the waste supply chain.

For the first time, our water regulation teams completed more than 10,000 inspections of water company assets in a single year, identifying permit breaches in 22% of cases. This has built a clear, evidence-based picture of non-compliance which will shape our future regulation.

By equipping our regulatory teams with better tools, we are enabling them to make stronger use of data and insights. One example is a new digital system that will make it easier for our officers to record, track and manage noncompliance, improving follow up on actions from previous inspections. This Regulatory Compliance Service (RCS) is already in use across our Water Quality inspections and will soon roll out to other sectors including waste.
Across all sectors, we are also developing new regulation plans that focus on the real-world outcomes we want our regulation to achieve.

We are striving to provide clear, proportionate and predictable regulation. That means reducing uncertainty and enabling investment by stepping back where risks are low, taking an evidence-based approach where they’re higher, and acting firmly when needed. For example, in waste, we are setting new minimum inspection frequencies for different types of sites, focusing our effort on poor performers and high‑risk sites whilst reducing routine regulatory activity at consistently well performing sites.
Strengthening our regulatory profession

Whilst we are accelerating our use of digital, data and AI, I firmly believe that people remain at the heart of good regulation. That’s why we are strengthening regulation across the Environment Agency by establishing a Regulation Profession and investing in the learning, development and infrastructure needed to support them.

Through accredited training and new pathways with industry and academia, we are building a confident, skilled workforce supported by cutting-edge digital tools. In the waste sector for example, we are using AI and machine learning to strengthen compliance analytics, detect waste related risks and optimise assessments.
New approaches to drive progress

New approaches are key to driving progress. We’ve recently taken up the Lead Environmental Regulator position on four pilot projects – East West Rail, Lighthouse Green Fuels, Sizewell C and the Trelavour Lithium Project. This is providing developers with clearer, earlier, and more coordinated environmental guidance across environmental regulators, while maintaining robust protections.

We are also supporting innovation in areas like decarbonisation. Notable regulatory milestones include issuing the first UK refinery carbon capture and storage (CCS) permit and securing the VPI Immingham carbon capture permit - both enabling significant industrial decarbonisation.
Through our commitment to proportionate regulation and delivering environmental outcomes, we’re taking firm action where risks are high while exploring opportunities to step back where risks are low.

The Earned Autonomy programme is one example. We're working with trusted partners such as the Rivers Trust, National Trust and Forestry Commission to deliver nature recovery projects faster and more efficiently, while developing new standard rule permits, increasing exemptions, and working towards a Nature Recovery Regulatory Position Statement. A recent Regulatory Position Statement (RPS) for low-risk abstraction for nature recovery actions and fish or eel passage builds on an earlier low-risk impounding works RPS, allowing a more proportionate, risk-based approach that removes unnecessary barriers to habitat restoration, nature recovery and natural flood management projects.
Looking ahead

Our ambition is a regulatory system that is digitally enabled, risk-driven, transparent and easier to navigate. By combining better data, stronger regulatory capability and smarter technology, we can target our efforts where they achieve the greatest environmental outcomes while providing greater certainty for those we regulate.

While our transformation is by no means complete, action is underway. We have a clear understanding of what needs to be done. Independent reviews by important bodies such as the Office for Environmental Protection and the National Audit Office, alongside recommendations from Dan Corry and John Fingleton, continue to act as catalysts for change.

Lasting change cannot be delivered by the Environment Agency alone. It depends on Government setting new policies and reforming legislation and on those we regulate working with us towards a shared ambition of better environmental outcomes.

There is far more happening than I can cover in one blog. In the coming months, I will publish my next Chief Regulator report, providing a detailed overview of progress against our EA2030 strategy and the vision I outlined in my previous report.
Please follow the Chief Regulator’s LinkedIn page for further updates.
